Some days ago I drew
the attention of the Prime Minister to hardships that were being experienced by Canadians returning from the United States through their children being detained at the border. I mentioned the case of the wife of a Canadian soldier who was visiting her father in Brooklyn, New York, and who arrived at the Canadian boundary with a child six months of age, but was refused admission to Canada because she had not a certificate of health for the child as required by the Interior Department. The objection I saw Iwas that instead , of returning the mother to a distant point in the United States some arrangement might have been made by which the child might have been examined at the border. This occurred at MacAdam Junction. When the case was drawn to my attention I laid it before the Prime Minister who said he would submit it to the Minister of the Interior. Would the minister explain how the matter stands and if anything has been done to relax the rule first adopted in regard to this matter?

speakeroldname: Hon. W. J. ROCHE (Minister of Interior) :
speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
In reading the hon. gentleman's
remarks in Hansard I gathered the opinion that the was undetr the impression that this was a medical examination enforced against immigrants coming into Canada. That is not the case. The hon. gentleman will remember that last fall there was a very severe epidemic of infantile paralysis particularly in the city and state of New York, which spread to the other neighbouring states, and spme of the United States municipalities had actually an embargo against their city of New York. For the protection of our children in Canada it was considered necessary to have an embargo placed against those -states in which infantile paralysis was epidemic, we therefore insisted upon any person coming into Canada with children having a certificate from a medical doctor that the children had not 'been exposed to any case of infantile paralysis within thirty days. The transportation Companies were informed as to this requirement, so that any person purchasing tickets to Canada was or should have been informed by the ticket agent as to the necessity of providing certificates of this kind. My hon. friend will see that it would be of no use to have Canadian medical mem at the boundary to give such certificates. I may say, however, that this embargo has been removed by reason of the suppression of the infantile paralysis epidemic.

speechtext: On motion of Sir Robert Bordem (Prime Minister) Bill No. 24, for granting to His Majesty aid for military and naval defence was read for the second time, and the House went into Committee thereon, Mr Rainville in the Chair.

Mr. Speaker,
before this Bill is passed, I wish to enter once more -my protest against this policy which is ruining the people of this country.
I may state, that il am not at variance with the ends pursued by the Allies, but solely with the manner in which this war is managed by the Government.
Hon. gentlemen possibly may enquire whether I am alone holding such views. In answer, I might quote from some London papers, -statements to the effect that Great Britain, during the year 1915, would never ask for 150,000 men from Canada, realizing that such a sacrifice would be too heavy for us; and, in those papers, it was further stated that Canadians working in the fields

were helping the Allies' cause as much as those who were fighting in the trenches'.
Furthermore;, Mr. Speaker, .quite recently a French lieutenant, after spending twenty-eight months in the trenches, haying returned to Canada, on leave, to recuperate, made the following statement:
" On learning that Canada was to send forward 33,000 men, we said to ourselves: what a noble deed? When, later on, we were informed that a second contingent was to he sent overseas, we considered it as a sublime act of patriotism. When, still later on, in January, 1916, the Prime Minister of Canada stated that he would send
500,000	men, we exclaimed: That is madness ! "
Now,* Mr. Speaker, such being the case, it seems to .me that Canada having .sent to the front 50,000, 75,000, or even 100,000 men at $1.10 per day, might have -stopped and taken up the manufacturing of munitions, though not for the exclusive benefit of the friends of the Government, but in every Canadian centre; and moreover might have utilized Government works for the manufacturing of munitions at cost price, or at a nominal advance of 10 or 15 per cent, whereas it is found that scandalous profits of 400 and 900 per cent have been secured thereon by friends of the Government.
I repeat it, the Government might well *have made use of their own plants to turn out war munitions, and supply work to all comers for the purpose of meeting the requirements of the Allies. What happened since this war has broken out? What was the slogan of Lloyd George, the present Prime Minister, when addressing the House of Commons a short time ago? Munitions, munitions, munitions! In fact, this wax is nothing else but a war of munitions and guns. So much so, that Great Britain, after sending men over to France to fight in the trenches, recalled home a number of them to turn out munitions instead. Such being the case, I afh not at all certain, as a business man and a merchant, and also as the head of a family who has provided for his children by holding the plough, I am not at all certain, I say, whether this Government is doing the right thing towards the people of this country, by sending over to France and Flanders, to wage war, Canadian boys at $1.10 a day, when Great Britain has as many recruits as she is able to send over at one shilling a day. In the meantime, Great Britain is bound to keep at home a fairly large number of men physically fit, for the purpose of turning out munitions. Once more, may I inquire why

Canada should commit the egregious mistake of sending her men overseas, instead of keeping them .here to turn out munitions for the Allies, who are so much in. need of them.
Mr. Speaker, I stated last year in this House and throughout my constituency whenever an opportunity offered, that if it could be shown that by means of 200,000 men drafted from Canada, we might win the war, I would not dbject to our making such a sacrifice. But, considering that Russia, with a man power of twenty-five or thirty million men, has not enough rifles or munitions to equip one third of that num

ber, while here in Canada we are in need of all onr people, I believe, Mr. Speaker, it is high time to put a stop to this- sending of troops overseas. We have thinned our ranks to quite a sufficient extent; we have sent over rifles, though they are not any too good, if we are to judge from the statements made in this House for a few days past.
There must have been something in the wind last year, when the right hon. .Prime Minister shot his bolt about sending 500,000 -men. It is not my intention to cast any aspersions on him, 'but if we are to judge from the speeches which have been delivered on the Address, it is -quite credible that its intent was to enable some fanatics, such as the hon. member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards), to impugn the province of Quebec and assert that she is not living up to her obligations. Mr. Speaker, it is claimed that the province of Quebec it not fulfilling its duty. What happened when the war broke cut? Frenchmen answered their country's call; so did the Belgians. Should not . Englishmen who have been here for one, five, or even fifteen years, have answered as well the call of their Mother Country? Such was not the case, however. A number of them enlisted in the .Canadian army at $1.10 per day, because the pay was higher with us than at home, and they are welcome to it. The province of Quebec has not received .many immigrants from the British Isles; the greater pant of these have gone to Ontario and the West. Is it not a matter of course that these people being newcomers in Canada, should answer their country's call, as recruits either for the British or the Canadian contingents? These late arrivals reading in the newspapers that the Huns had thrown bombs on British unfortified cities, were impelled to enlist with the object of defending their relatives at home.	.
As regards enlisting in the two provinces of Ontario and Quebec, comparisons be-

tween these two provinces are not in order, for the reasons I have stated. If reports in the press are to be credited, Ontario claims
110,000	British born, out of a total of 152,000 enlistments. How many are there in the province of Quebec? I cannot say, but there should not be many of them, British immigrants having kept aloof of our province.
Moreover, I say that this vexed question as regards- enlistments, which is being constantly thrown in our faces, with the object of showing that the province of Quebec Is disloyal, is very despicable business. It should not be brought up in this House, and- the right -hon. the Prime Minister should refuse to countenance any attempt of that kind.
-Now, I shall take up another point. I was surprised: to hear the hon. Minister of Finance, in his speech of January 30 last, refer to the country's prosperity, to the fabulous figures our exports have reached to, an cl in a general to the prosperous state of business. Qf course, I have not been trained to -speech-making, neither have I presided- over trusts; I -am only a -farmer and a merchant. However, -I am aware that when a town corporation or a school board in the .province of Quebec make up their -minds to borrow $1,500 or $2,000, they are called upon to refund the amount within twelve months, or even within thirty or ninety -days. Now, I wonder whether the Minister of Finance at whose request the House voted 800 millions for 1917-18, would be in a position to refund that amount within ninety days, as the aforesaid corporations do. I believe that the people of this -country, who are being deceived day in and day -out -by the government organs, would consider tha-t the war -comes high, should the Minister of Finance some -day come out with some, such statement: We are in need of 800 millions, and the loan will -have to -be refunded within ninety days. In the province of Quebec, families with ten or twelve children -are no exception, and they have to be provided for in -any ca-se. I wonder whether the people would take -stock in any -statement made by the minister or his -colleagues, a-s regards the prosperity of the country, if the head of a family, with ten or twelve children to provide for, were called upon to contribute $1,400. How could the people of this country foot the bill? There would not be found 25 per -cent in -a position tc liberate themselves-. The ministers hailing from the province of Quebec went through that province last year and attempted to make the people believe that we
were actually prosperous, though it is known that it is all the outcome of the manufacturing of shells and gun-s, with the object of making -fo-dder for guns, -as the ministers themselves asserted in 1910. So I say that we should not rely on that prosperity, which is only fictitious, and will be a source of disappointment, once the war is over.
Mr. Speaker, before closing my remarks, I wish to -call your -attention to a question which i-s being mooted: I mean conscription. La Patrie, of Montreal, suggested yesterday that it might be enacted very soon. Whatever will be the outcome of it, Mr. Speaker,. I wish to state right here that I a-m not in favour of conscription, not any more than I am in favour of sending men overseas. I repeat it, if the Government had at heart the interests of the people, the Prime Minister, previous to embarking for Europe, would- state in this House that recruiting will stop at once, in order to enable the youths of Ontario to remain in that province, and the young men an other parts of Canada to remain also where they -are, including those from St. Rose, in the county of Dorchester, who were called upon to -cross the -boundary, -should ever conscription be enacted. Of -co-ur.se, should the United States enter the war, these people might be induced to return home.' So I say that it is incumbent on the Prime Minister to state that -conscription will not become law, and that voluntary enlistments will .continue to -be the rule. We should keep oair own in the country, to raise crops of -all kind-s, and to turn out butter, cheese -and all the foodstuffs required for the provisioning of the Allies.
Mr. -Speaker, I -shall not -delay the House any longer, reserving my right to take up the subject anew when the budget comes under dicussion.

Mr. Chairman, I am sure that the House must regret, in view of the adjournment to-morrow, that the Government in introducing this measure, which in its general nature has the support of the House in its entirety, has not seen fit to give some information to those who are particularly interested in Ithe welfare of the boys overseas as to the 'statements made in the report of Dr. Bruce, and in the report of Dr. Baptie and his colleagues with reference to the statements of Dr. Bruce. In the press of the country there have appeared from time to time excerpts from these reports, and certain statements have been made of a nature to excite the

public mind with reference to them; but, so far as the House is concerned, we have not received any information whatever. It is true that an order of the House was passed for the laying on the Table of both these reports, but, so far, that order has not been complied with. I submit that there is no valid reason why it should not have been complied with, because I have no doubt whatever that these reports were contained in printed documents which were in the hands of the Prime Minister, or the Minister of Militia, and could have been placed upon the table of the House without any difficulty whatever. It would be in the public interest to know exactly what the statements were, and to know what the real situation is in regard to this very important matter. I hope that before we adjourn to-morrow, the Government will, for the satisfaction of those who are intensely interested in this matter, give the House and the country the exact reports as they have come to them from the different bodies that have been making these investigations.
If one is to judge from the newspaper reports in regard to these matters, Dr. Bruce, about whose standing there is absolutely no question, was appointed by the Government for the purpose of making an examination into the medical conditions which existed on the other side. As I have said, about his standing and ability there can be no question. In these newspaper reports we find it stated that there was no medical inspection of Canadian soldiers in the military hospitals in England by the Canadian Medical Service, that there was no efficient medical inspection of any kind made of our men in the Canadian hospitals, previous to the time when Dr. Bruce took up his duties and made his report. If that statement is correct, it seems to me that a very grave state of affairs indeed is disclosed. We have there the men who have been wounded in France, taken to England, and distributed among the various hospitals all over Great Britain, and yet we are told that they were under no supervision or inspection by the medical men who went over from Canada. Dr. Bruce is authority for the statement that no inspection whatever by any recognized Canadian medical officers was made of those men of ours who were in the military hospitals, and that no efficient inspection of any kind was made by our men of those who were in the Canadian hospitals. As has been pointed out in the newspaper reports, the consequence has been that soldiers have 
been retained in hospitals who should have returned to duty, thus disclosing gross neglect in the whole matter. The newspapers state that men were retained who should have been returned to duty; and that a great many others should have been returned to ' Canada where they could have been more economically treated. What is the answer to this? Is the House and the country not to know whether or not these statements are true? My hon friend the ex-Minister of Militia (Sir Sam Hughes) went to Toronto shortly before his resignation, and was reported in the Toronto press as having stated that our Canadian soldiers were allowed to come under the knife of first year medical men in charge of the hospitals in England, when qualified doctors were available.
I never said first year medical men; if I did I meant first year doctors after they had graduated.
I assume that my hon. friend will refer to this matter. I am merely quoting from an extract in a Toronto paper.
I never read it.
It gives his address in Toronto.
I never heard of the statement before.
I am simply taking it from the report in the Toronto newspaper.
What paper?
The Toronto Mail.
Of what date?
My hon. friend can satisfy his curiosity by looking it up in the library.

I am not finding any fault with the hon. member. I may have used the words which he quotes; I will not say that I did not use them, but what was in my mind, and what we objected to, was that first year doctors, not students, should have been put in charge of these hospitals.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: First year after graduation?
Yes, some of them within six weeks of graduation.
That is what^this report states that my hon. friend said, first year medical men."
You said first year students before that.
I did not call them students; I read to the House what my hon. friend was reported to have said.

What the country
is particularly interested in is not what my hon. friend was unable to accomplish in regard to this matter, but whether or not the condition of affairs reported by Dr. Bruce existed in England. That is a matter which I assume my hon. friend can discuss.
This report also discloses the very important fact that many soldiers had been sent to England who were unfit and who should not have been enlisted at all. That statement implies a lack of care and of proper management on the part of the medical service of the Militia Department. If large numbers of men were enlisted and sent to England without proper examination, to become a charge upon the country, it will be agreed that it is another very improper condition of affairs. It is stated dn that report that in every battalion which arrived in England it was found after medical inspection that from five to fifteen per cent of the men -were medically unfit. An instance is given of a particular battalion, the Canadian Pioneer draft, which had 57 unfit men out of 254 which constituted the whole draft of officers and men.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
What is the
statement?
The statement is that the Canadian Pioneer draft, composed of 254 officers and men, had 57 men who were medically unfit for duty, and were pronounced to be unfit when they reached the other side.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: What date is that?
It is in the report of Dr. Bruce.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: At what date?

that it will cost $4,000,000 inclusive of all the other charges which go to make up the account. There are allegations made in regard to the question of sending men to what are known as V. A. D., or Voluntary Aid Detachment, hospitals. I think that some very worthy people raise the point that a great Imperial issue is at stake and that our Canadian boys should be practically compelled to go to the V. A. D. hospitals in order that their faith in the Empire may not he impaired. To say that the Imperial spirit of these poor Canadian boys will be impaired unless they are associated with and lie beside boys from other parts of the Dominion seems to me to he the veriest twaddle.
I did not catch that.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
My hon. friend has called attention to what is suggested in certain reports that are not yet before the House in their entirety, and are only known in so far as their contents have been published in the press. I may say that the printing is being expedited as much as possible. We cabled to Great Britain to ascertain whether any printed copies of the Bruce report were available, and we are informed that forty copies have been mailed. The other report, as I have said, is being printed with all possible expedition. I do not purpose entering into a discussion of the reports before they are on the table of the House and can be examined in their entirety, but some of the suggestions made by my hon. friend are worthy of a moment's attention.
With regard to the lack of inspection of Canadians in Imperial hospitals, I am not qualified to speak from a medical standpoint nor as having any special experience in such matters; but I suppose that the inspection of Canadians in such hospitals would be left to the Imperial authorities, just as the inspection of Imperial soldiers in Canadian hospitals would doubtless be left to the Canadian medical authorities who have control of such hospitals.
My hon. friend has spoken as if the medical service overseas, whether in British hospitals or in Canadian hospitals, was of a very inferior character.
I quoted Dr. Bruce's report.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I think it is most undesirable to spread an impression of that kind amongst the people of this country. I visited forty-three hospitals,

Canadian and British, last year, and I did not see one of them that, so far as I could judge, was not well organized and well carried on, I saw the Canadian hospitals in England; I saw a very large number of British hospitals, and I found the medical men and others in charge of those hospitals keenly alive to their responsibilities and anxious to do everything possible for the comfort of the men under their care.
Dr. Bruce does not say so.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
ahead at the end of the day. I was told that a large number of lumbermen in one of the battalions were being rejected for the reason that they had flat feet. It seems to me that it would be desirable to try these men out, and see whether in endurance upon the inarch they would not be quite as capable as others who in this respect would be accepted for enlistment. The memorandum which my hon. friend asked for some time ago as to the unfit enlisted for overseas service has been placed in my hands, by the Deputy Minister of Militia and is:
The records of the department show that the following were returned to Canada during the years 1915 and 1916 as being medically unfit: 2,701 in the year 1915; 3,651 in the year 1916.
These figures, of course, include a number who left Canada fit, but who contracted disease during their training in England. The figures for 1915 also include any wounded returned that year.
The balance of those not found fit for service at the front, such as those with slight defects, over age, etc., are being retained for light duty in England, and it is also understood that two Construction Battalions have been organized from these men.
As to the cost, it will not be possible to state the cost with any degree of accuracy without taking up each individual case, owing to the varying periods of service and the various ranks held, and this would take months to furnish.
The estimated cost per man in the Canadian Expeditionary Force is $1,000 a year.
My hon. friend asked also with regard to No. 7 Hospital and No. 8 Hospital. No.
7 Hospital is at Le Treport, in France. I do not remember the exact complaint made with regard to Le Treport Hospital. I visited that hospital last year on my way from Paris to Folkestone. I spent the greater part of a day there, and, as far as I could judge, the hospital seemed to be well organized. Has my hon. friend any particular information as to its defects?
How many cots are there in that hospital?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I really do not remember the number of cots; it is a very large hospital. In fact, there are two hospitals there. One is a British hospital, which is located in a very large hotel overlooking the sea and which was built, I wai * n formed, by a German syndicate a year or two before the war. Shortly after the war broke out it was expropriated by the French Government and placed at the disposal of the British authorities. It is a very large and well-equipped hospital. The Canadian hospital was located in tents and huts im-

mediately adjoining. There were a large number of patients in the hospital when 1 was there, and a large staff of nurses was employed. The hospital was under the command of Lieutenant Colonel Bridges who was attached to the Canadian Permanent Force.
That was near Dieppe?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
At Treport. I recollect that when I first went to France there was a gathering of the officers of all the Canadian hospitals in that vicinity, officers from the staffs of five Canadian hospitals, including the hospital at Treport; and there was present, also, the chief medical officer in the British "service who had jurisdiction over the district in which these hospitals were situated. The highest possible compliment was paid to the organization of the Canadian hospitals by that officer in speaking at a dinner which was given by Lieutenant Colonel Murray McLaren and the officers under his command.
No. 8 hospital is at St. Cloud, near Paris, France.
The number of beds laid down for general hospitals is 1,040, with an establishment of 46 officers, 73 nursing sisters, and 201 n.c.o.'s and men.
It, however, frequently happens that after an hospital has been located, the accommodation is from time to time increased, and as a consequence, the staff. There is no information available in Canada as to the present standing in this respect of the hospital at Treport. If particular information is required it will have to be obtained from overseas.
No. 7 is at present used for the accommodation of casualties of the British Expeditionary Forces.
No. 8 was offered by the Canadian Government to the French Government, as a complimentary contribution towards the cost of France's share of the war, to be used for the accommodation of French casualties, but it remains under Canadian control.
Both these hospitals are doing exceedingly good work.
I asked Colonel Mignault, who had to do with the establishment of No. 8 hospital, to give a statement with regard to it some time ago, and I might read one or two quotations from a letter which he has written to me on this subject. He said:

No. 8 Canadian Hospital was sent to France on the 23rd of November, 1915. It took the months of December, January and February to erect it, on the Racing Course at 'St. Cloud, property of Mr. Blanc. It is built with barracks which were furnished by the French army at a cost of 250,000 fr., but put up by our own men.
On the 1st of March, 1916, the hospital was ready to receive patients, and on the 17th of the same month, the first trainload of wounded from Verdun reached us, and then the hospital was filled up rapidly. It -has a capacity of five hundred and twenty (520)
heds.	..	.
Hospitals in France are divided into three categories, namely A, B, and C, according to the importance and seriousness of cases. Thus, Class A stands for "Les grands blessOs"; Class B for "Les blessds moyens," and Class C
for "Des petits blessds. '
Three hospitals are classified m Paris in Class A. One is the Val de Grace Hospital in Paris (1,000 beds). The second is the American Hospital (600 beds), which is kept up by the generosity of individuals of the great Republic. The third one is the St. Cloud Hospital, No. 8 Canadian General.
So this stands among the three chief hospitals of Paris at the present time, according to the report given to me by Colonel Mignault. Colonel Mignault continues in his 'letter:
The above-named three hospitals are the only ones classified in Class A, that is to say, they are SO thoroughly equipped with surgical appl -ances, etc., as to be able to take care of all cases, whatever may be their severity or their importance.
With regard to segregation or otherwise of the Canadian wounded, I do not think that there ought to be a policy for segregation or a policy against it. I think that these matters must be determined according to the military exigencies. There is a great deal to toe said in favour of Canadians toeing among their own people and living under the care of Canadian nuTses. On the other hand, I think there is much to be said for that fellowship and _ comradeship which comes from the association of men from this Dominion with, men from the Old Country and from the other Dominions in hospitals and convalescent homes. I saw Canadians in our own hospitals; I saw them in British hospitals in many parts of the country; but I never .found any complaint whatever from any Canadian or from any soldier in any hospital with respect to the care and attention which he was receiving, and I have heard no complaint from any Canadian who was in a British hospital as to his desire to 'be placed elsewhere. It may toe that some of them would like to be more among their own people. That is quite possible, because I know they were very glad indeed to see
the face and hear the voice of some one from home.
With regard to what my hon. friend has said respecting Witley Camp, the statements which he has made come to me for the first time. If he will give me further particulars I ehall make it my business to inquire and to see that any such condition is remedied.
What is that point?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: He said that although a Canadian officer at Witley Camp desired that the canteen should be closed for the welfare of his men, the British contractor, who had some authority from the War Office, disregarded his wishes and insisted upon keeping the canteen open. I think the desire ot a Canadian officer in respect of such a matter ought to be respected, and I shall be very glad to take the matter up.

I shall very gladly
give to the Prime Minister the name of the officer who gives me that information, but if my right hon. friend thinks that the whole question is whether the wish or will of that particular officer who was the orderly officer of the day should be respected is the issue involved in that question he is much mistaken. I fail to see for one moment what possible right the British Government has to lease to any contractor over there the right to sell whisky and rum to Canadian soldiers in a Canadian camp, or to do anything else in a Canadian camp. That is the question involved, and in that regard the problem is very much larger than the mere question of whether the orderly officer of the day is to have his authority flouted and disregarded by a man who happens to be a contractor.
My right hon. friend suggests that there should be no discussion of the Bruce and Baptie reports until the reports come down.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I did not say
that. I said we could discuss it more effectively.	[DOT]

Let us see what the facts in this matter are. This examination of Dr. Bruce's into the Canadian hospitals, according to the information which has unquestionably come from governmental sources, was inaugurated by the ex-Minister of Militia, and the report of Dr. Bruce was made to the ex-minister previous to his retirement.

Made to the then
Minister of Militia.
%

This is technical, I will accept that. This was made to the Minister of Militia, not in England or the acting Overseas Minister of Militia in England; it was made to Major General Sir Sam Hughes, Minister of Militia of the Dominion of Canada, before he resigned last fall. Now for what reason or purpose does my right hon. friend come here and, in the month of February, 1917, and as an excuse for not presenting that departmental report to the House, say that he is waiting until he receives some copies of the report from England? And then he undertakes to intimate to me that it is most undesirable for me to discuss this question, when that report must be in the possession of this Government, must be here in Ottawa, and must have been here for some time.
My right hon. friend, having had before him a report which he does not bring to Parliament, introduced a commission presided over by Sir William Baptie which goes out and examines this report of Dr. Bruce's. Again I assume that the report of Sir William Baptie with re erence to the statements made by Dr. Bruce is in the possession of the Government. And yet my right hon. friend intimates that it is undesirable that we should discuss it in this House. How long are we to wait before these reports are brought down? It seems to me that we are the last people on earth 'before whom this Government desires to place anything. Statements are given out to the press, but nothing is given to Parliament, and we are told it is not desirable to discuss these things in Parliament. It is said to be undesirable to open one's mouth in regard to the interests of the boys overseas. That seems to me a most remarkable position to take. There are many people in this country who hiave no kith or kin at the front, who are very good at lecturing people who say a word on behalf of the boys who have gone overseas. So far as I am concerned, I do not propose to take lecturing from people of that sort. The men who have gone overseas look to us as representatives of the constituencies in Parliament to ascertain the facts in regard to conditions overseas. Mhat is the good of my right hon. friend saying that a certain number of K.C.M.G.'s sat on a commission to consider Dr. Bruce's report? We know that Dr. Bruce is a Canadian surgeon of high standing, that no one would venture to impute anything against him. That being so, he having made two or three charges in regard to the administration of the hospitals of this Canadian Gov-

ernment overseas, the representatives of the people, speaking for the boys who have gone overseas, I submit have a right to discuss this question before Parliament. It is our duty to find out what these reports were and what the truth was. My right hon. friend has not told us just where we stand in regard to this matter. What answer is it to give to the mothers and fathers of the boys who have gone overseas to say that a gentleman with K.C.M.G. tacked to his name has sat on a committee land made a report that we have not yet had placed before us in Parliament? That is where we are in regard to this question.
I submit that this House is entitled to some expression of opinion by the responsible Government of this country as to whether or not they regard the statements of Dr. Bruce's report as having been true, and whether or not they regard the statements of Sir William Baptie's report as true. That is the situation in regard to the men overseas, and that is what I want to know.	[DOT]

The matter of the canteen has come up. When the Canadian division went to England first, in the fall of 1914, I crossed over, and, in my innocence under the British military law and under the Canadian military law, I thought that I had some say still in the affairs of our troops. I was politely informed that I had nothing whatever to do with the canteen or rationing or feeding of the men, that General Alderson had let that to certain English contractors, and that Canada had no right to interfere, as it w.as outside our military .sphere, that the contracts had been let to some company not only for the Canadians, but for the forces in England, and that .contracts could not 'be interfered with. I protested against it. We had learned at Valcartier that as much as $33,000 in one case had been made by one of the contractors in a period of six weeks, and there were upwards of one hundred of these gentlemen. It was the first time that we learned that so much money was being distributed. We set to work to run the canteens under regimental boards, and the result was a saving of upwards of $1,000 a month. There is a regimental fund, money belonging, to the men themselves for their own distribution and maintenance. I wanted this plan carried out.
Did they not try to institute a dry canteen over in England?

I will come to that in a minute. I tried to institute a dry canteen, and I was informed in a gentlemanly way that I had no jurisdiction. General Alderson told the men with a great hurrah and bravado in the only speech he ever made except when he read to them a little book which he once published about how not to do things
Who was that?
General Alderson. He told them he was going to make them free men and, as a slap at the Minister of Militia in Canada, he said he was going to give them a wet canteen.

Is it not the fact that liquor is given to the men every day in the trenches? I have heard objection made in Montreal by parents who would not allow their sons to go over there because they were afraid that they would get into the . habit of taking liquor which they had not been in the habit of taking before they went away.

In the trenches, when men are standing up to their waists in water, they get a little rum, not as a beverage, but as a stimulant; and, although I may be regarded as a fairly temperate man, I certainly would not object to any officer, non-commissioned officer, or man getting his tot of rum, as they call it, when he is standing up to the waist in water in the trenches.
Is this done at all times, or only when they are about to go into action?
I am not discussing that question.
I am merely asking for information.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My hon. friend's (Mr. Marcil) remarks might be misconstrued. I have never heard that the rum is given to the men when they are going into action. What I have heard is that when men are exhausted, and wet and cold, a very small proportion of rum is given to them merely as a stimulant, for the time being, to prevent unfortunate results from cold and wet. As to rum being given to men going into action, that is something I have never heard of, and I do not believe it for one moment.
I understand that it is the practice to give the men a little liquor in the trenches-

In South Africa
where the climate is very hot, we had rum issued to us, but we never used it except when going into some hazardous exercise. I have no hesitation in saying that when the boys wanted it they could get it. If I were running the show to-day, I would say that when men are standing in the trenches up to their waists in water-and I think I can claim to be as practical a temperance man as there is in Canada-I would have no objection to them having their tot of rum. I regard it, under these conditions, as a medicine and npt as a beverage. This extraordinary piffle about rum being handed out in the trenches, and all that sort of thing, comes from people who do not understand what they are talking about, and who are simply trying to create an agitation in that regard. I take second place to no man in Canada in supporting the cause of temperance, but I do not like any of this piffle served up when the boys are fighting and dying in the trenches.
Another question which has come up is the question of fallen instep. There are three grades of fallen instep, as I am told by medical men. In the third grade the men are really unfit, and I do not think there are many of that class sent over. There was one fellow who came into Edmonton and was rejected. He wrote to me, and I had a doctor examine him. He had walked from Peace River to Edmonton, and yet he was rejected as unfit. However, I sent him ovier, and he was rejected over there. He told them that I had sent him, and I arranged that he should go to the front. He went into the trenches, and is one of the best marchers to be found anywhere. Any man accustomed to wearing moccasins is certain to suffer from fallen instep. Nearly all the woodmen are in the habit of wearing moccasins and they often suffer from a fallen instep. I think that the medical regulations should have been relaxed a little in that respect, and I did relax them in the case of two or three who were in the first and second stages of fallen instep, but in The third stage a man cannot march very far.
Then there is the question of segregation, which has been referred to by the Prime Minister. I think that if he reads Dr. Bruce's report the right hon. gentleman will see that he himself agrees exactly with Dr. Bruce. I have not read the rfiport, but Dr. Bruce talked over the matter with me and bis views and those of the Prime Minister are exactly the same. I look at the matter purely from a business point of view.

I could never see why our men should be hauled from say Folkestone to the north of Scotland, when we have hospitals of the right class near Folkestone where they cou'd get better service and where 340 or $50 could be saved in each case over sending them to other places. Nox could I see why our men should be .sent to the V.A.D. hospitals. These hospitals axe presided over by the most charming women in tire world; I am not saying a word against them-such nice little girls with five or six weeks' training in 'some St. John's Ambulance affair or something of that kind - s helpers; the dearest little creatures in the world for smoothing brows and holding hands,-but J did object to Canadian soldiers being sent there, and to paying three shillings a day to keep our boys when we had our own highly skilled nurses. The hands of our skilled nurses might be a little rougher, and not so smooth on the brow, but I wanted our boys to get the attendance which could be given by our own nurses who had had >at least three years of experience itn our hospitals. That is what Dt. Bruce objected to, and that is what I object to. He also objected to having our men kept there when they should -be in the trenches. There was one of these V. A. D. hospitals that had a baseball team as you will find it mentioned in the report 'and the men were kept playing baseball when they should have been in the trenches. When Dr. Bruce w.as examining these hospitals- Colonel Jones, or General Jones, managed to rake up in a very small circle around London, 700 men, and shoved them back into convalescent camps immediately. In 1915 when I was over there and when the Prime Minister was over there, I inspected a battalion at Sbormcliffe one day. They had -only about 200 men. I asked for the parade state, and it showed that there were about 1,200 men. I wanted to know where they were, and I was told that so many were convalescent-, and so many were here, and so many were there. I said, "What are these convalescents doing here, they should not he here." I said that we wanted no men in the battalion except fit men, and so I ordered that the convalescents should be kept all in one place by themselves, and not mixed up with the rest of the camp, the plan being to have them in one camp and divided into six or seven classes, those just out of the hospital, those convalescing, and so on in the various stages up to the last class which would be fit to go back to their battalion and take their places in 
the trenches. That was the plan which we arranged and carried out until the new overseas minister sent them back, I understand ; and now they are rambling all around England. We had hundreds and hundreds of men rambling around England. We were returning from 8 to 10 per cent of our men. while the British regulars were returning about 60 per cent and Kitchener's mein were returning about 30 per cent until I arranged that convalescent plan. Then in the similar periods we returned 60 per cent. I am not reflecting on General Jones-I want to let him out-but if this agitation is going to be carried on by the V. A. D. people, fourth grade society dames in London, the facts are going to come out. I do not want to hurt General Jones; I have stuck to him as far as I can.
Has the ex-minister read the letter written by Lady Drummond on that subject?

Lady Drummond
sent me several letters. I am not aware that Lady Drummond or any other society lady wias authorized to run our hospitals'. There was also Sir William Osier; he wrote several letters. The dear creatures who hang around the outskirts of society in England wrote a great many letters, and interfered, but I was not aware that it was any of their business. I thought that Canada should manage her own affairs. All the agitation has come from these hand-holders and brow-rubbers.
What about Genera1 Jones?

When I got to England in 1915, and knowing that the Prime Minister was desirous of visiting the hospitals, I got General Jones to furnish for him a 'list of the hospitals where the boys who had been wounded at St. Julien were placed. It took three weeks to get the list, but I got it and gave it to the Prime Minister. It stated that there were about 200 of the boys at Cardiff. On the way there I happened to get off at Oxford to have a look around, and I found fifteen or sixteen men there. I met one boy who had just the day before passed the " cannot recover " stage, and he said that as soon as he was well again !he was going hack to the trenches. I said, " You will he of no use in the trenches," He said, " I cannot'get cold feet because I have only one foot to get cold." I have seen him since tripping along with a cork leg, about as good looking a boy as

there ie in the country. At Cheltenham, I found a Canadian nurse and a number of Canadians in the hospital there. The name of not one of them was on the list of General Jonee. At Cardiff, I found that there were three Canadians in the hospital, whereas 200 were reported on the list. At Aberystwyth I found a number not reported, and I saw that by following Jonee' .report I would not get 'anything, 'and I paid no further attention to it. I was looking ait the matter from the business end, and the convalescent system .that I established in 1915 during the first year saved1 Canada $6,000,000, by restoring men, to the fighting line who otherwise would have been lying in hospitals in England holding hands and having their brows smoothed as I have pointed out. The very first day on which I let Dr. Bruce loose in England, 700 men were picked up and sent back, and every week they kept going back. There was no system of getting reports about these men at all until I established the convalescent system. I told the Prime Minister this; I told him that Jones' statement was no good. In 1916 I went over intending to look after the business.end of things; I was not interfering with the medical end. I challenge any members of this House to find in Dr. Bruce's report any criticism of the doctors. There is an etiquette among doctors, which I am sorry to say, is not observed among politicians, that they must not blackguard or expose each other. I could not induce the doctor for love or money to expose any malpractices. I could not get him to expose those fellows at ail.
Perhaps there were none.

I am not saying anything about that. However, I could not get Dr. Bruce to make any report on that aspect of the ease. I do not say that there were many cases of that kind but he would not touch the matter. What he reported on was the way in which we could bring about an improvement in the operation of the hospitals. I selected Dr. Bruce in order to reorganize the business end of the service. The year before I had taken up the financial end of it. I do not know that it interested me very much to hear the hon. Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White) tell the House the other day-it seemed a sort of a left-handed compliment-that he found things pretty good over there. I did not appreciate him telling me that, because I knew that things were good over there. I
knew that the medical end of it under Dr. Bruce would be improved over there and that it would be pretty good here too. The right hon. the First Minister has given us a comparison of a lot of extracts from the statements of those fellows; they are all good chaps-those Canadian officers who had to do with the Canadian end of it. I picked out Col. Ashton as a fighting officer. I did not know what he was as a medical officer but I knew he was a good fighting officer. Col. Fotheringham is a good man; Col. Ross, none better; Dr. Elder-the very best-he stands head and shoulders over Dr. Baptie in ability. Dr. McKeown, head of St. Michael's College, is one of the brightest men in Canada. He had a record unsurpassed in the history of the world for hospital work. Four or five of these gentlemen on Colonel Bruce's committee, I understand, are among the twelve Eedlowe of the Royal College of Surgeons of England living in Canada. There are Drs. Bruce, McKeown, Scott, and Hunter. Dr. Hunter is an Edinburgh man, now belonging to Winnipeg, who is one of the greatest physicians that it has been my privilege to meet. Dr. Wilson, I understand, comes from St. Catharines and he is one of the ablest and best administrators whom it has been my privilege to fall in with. Taking the Canadians on both lists, they are the pick of the fellows we have over there in the medical service. As far as Dr. Baptie is concerned, I am not going to say a word against him only that he may be a little prehistoric.
Were the gentlemen whom the hon. member has named, associated with Dr. Bruce in his examination?
Yes.
Dr. McKeown and the others?

Drs. McKeown,
Scott, Hunter and Wilson.
All good men.

There is nothing to touch them in Canada. I picked out the very best, the most highly qualified men that I could get. There is scarcely a man amongst those whom I have mentioned who had not a practice of from $30,000 to $150,000 in Canada. They gave their practices up to go over there. I do not know Dr. Baptie and I am not going to say anything agains't him, but, the fact that he was a medical officer in 1881 does net impress me a particle. He would naturally favour the

V.A.D. hospitals. That is where the whole trouble catne. Sir George Perley favoured the V.A.D. hospitals, but I did not feel that we were getting the best use of them. When the doctors would demand that the men should be sent to convalescent homes they would be told by the ladies in charge of them that they had been told by Dr. Carle-ton Jones that they should keep these men until others were sent to take their places. If others were not sent there immediately the men were kept because these places bad to be kept up. We were paying three shillings la day for these nurses,, while our own nurses were employed on English cases.

Who authorized Sir
George Perley to do that?
I did not anyway.
Will the hon. gentleman tell me if Dr. Bruce made a report directly to him as Minister of Militia?
He did.
When was that report received?
I do not remember exactly when it was received. It was in the month of September, but it is in the department and it will show.

I presume that report
is in the department and is available?
It was in the department when I was there. It was kept. The matter has never been taken up. I left the report there when I moved out.
We used to get many requests of that nature.

Does it not strike the exMinister of Militia as unusual that a man

who is fit for the trenches should be held back in a convalescent home?

Did he send his
mother the doctor's report that he is fit for the trenches?
He says he is fit.

Is not the hon.
gentleman aware that each man was passed first by the doctor of the battalion and that at Borden Camp every man was afterwards inspected by a full board of physicians? What further precautions could have been observed?
That is not speaking very highly of the ability of the physicians. Some of these men would have been rejected on their looks by any member of

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It chanced that I was in England at the time when the commission of inquiry was appointed by Sir George Perley and the Government. I am acquainted with the circumstances in which that action was taken. I may say that I have had some experience in connection with hospitals, and with members of the medical profession. For many years I was on the Senate and Board of Governors of the University of Toronto, For a considerable period I was one of the governors of the Toronto General Hospital. I was chairman of a committee at

one time which re-organized the staff of the Toronto General Hospital, and I then got to know something of the medical and surgical profession. I found that it was possible for doctors of the highest eminence to disagree, and- to disagree quite honestly. I know Dr. Bruce; he is a personal friend of mine, and a man of high standing in the Canadian surgical world. That is, I think, well known by all members of the House. When I went to England I found that Dr. Bruce, acting uppn the instructions of the ex-Minister of Militia, had made a report upon the hospital situation in Great Britain and was engaged in attempting to carry out the recommendations of that report, under instructions from the minister and, I believe, with the sanction of the Military Council which had been established in London. I found that great tension, very strong feeling, existed in London, as well as on the Continent, with regard to the Bruce report and his proceeding to carry it out. I took the opportunity of talking with men. high in the Canadian medical service, with officers and men of impartial judgment, and I found-I desire to make an absolutely fair statement respecting the matter-that while it was admitted that there were many good points in Dt. Bruce's report, it was in many respects impracticable to carry out its recommendations. I believe that is a fair statement of the opinion of the Canadian Medical Service and of official military opinion of London with respect to Dr. Bruce's report. I do not mean to say that that was a unanimous opinion. Dr. Bruce had some strong votaries and supporters; on the other hand, Dr. Jones had many equally strong votaries and supporters. I found the opinion prevailing very widely that Dr. Jones had been done some injustice, that the difficulties with which he had been obliged to contend bad not been taken into account, that as the war had developed burdens had been cast upon him and upon his organization, which had not been foreseen 'and which could not have been fully and adequately prepared against. We found the opinion prevailing widely among eminent members of the medical profession and among military men that Dr. Jones had done exceptionally well, having regard to all the circumstances surrounding his task. As I have said, it was thought by many-and in this I agreed-that there were many excellent points in Dr. Bruce's report. I believe that Dr. Bruce proceeded with his work in all good faith. He had not been a military man, 'and to that extent would not be acquainted with the practical difficulties
which might stand in the way of carrying out some of the recommendations which he made. In London 'a newspaper controversy had been proceeding with regard to the question of so-called segregation. Ilt was contended by some that Dr. Bruce's plan provided for the segregation of the Canadian troops-that the Canadian troops should not he allowed to mingle with the troops of Great Britain, Australia and New Zealand in the Canadian and British hospitals, But that they should be gathered together as Canadians in Canadian hospitals, and be treated by Canadian physicians and Canadian surgeons. I found a very strong feeling prevailing in London that it would be an unwise policy, an improper policy, 'to segregate the Canadians in their own hospitals and to deny to wounded British, Australian land New Zealand soldiers the privileges of Canadian hospitals. I think it is unfortunate that that controversy arose, because in reality-and I know that this is the opinion of Sir George Perley-the truth lies between the two extreme opinions. I do not regard it as necessary that Canadian soldiers, in twos, threes or groups of half a dozen, should be sent to remote parts of the United Kingdom for treatment. On the other hand I think it would be an unmixed misfortune, contrary to Canadian and Imperial interests, if a hard and fast rule were laid down that Canadian soldiers should be segregated in Canadian hospitals and not be allowed to mingle with the wounded soldiers of Great Britain, New Zealand and Australia. While I was in the United Kingdom I visited many Canadian and British hospitals. I took the time tp go about among the wards of those hospitals-I think it was one of the most interesting experiences of my life- and I asked many Canadians in those wards as to the treatment which they had experienced since becoming patients there and as to what they thought of the question of segregation. I state the substance of the answers truthfully to the committee when I say that, without any exception, they all spoke in the highest possible terms of the medical, surgical and nursing treatment which they had received in those hospitals. That was true also of the Canadian soldiers whom I saw in the British hospitals.
Having regard only to the main question of segregation, would the Canadian soldiers prefer to be segregated, or otherwise?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The Canadian
troops, according to the opinion of those

with whom I discussed the matter, would prefer a condition under which, while there would be a considerable number of Canadian soldiers in a hospital, there would also be soldiers of New Zealand, Australia, South Africa and Great Britain. I myself observed that here would be a Canadian in one bed, here an Australian next to him, there an Irishman and so on. I heard a story when I was at Cliveden that illustrated precisely what I have in mind. A Canadian was engaged in an animated discussion with an Australian about some matter over which they differed. It became heated, and the Irishman interposed in order to compose the difference. He said to the nurse: "This is the first time in the history of the world that an Irishman has been found making peace instead of breaking it." That is typical of what you find in all these hospitals. If in a hospital containing 1,000 beds there are two, three, four or five hundred Canadians, the Canadians will not be lonesome. On the other hand they do like to mingle with the Australians, the New Zealanders and the soldiers from the British Isles. It gives them a wider interest than they would otherwise have; it makes for breadth of view and of sympathy; an exchange of ideas continually goes on among these patients. I talked with hundreds of Canadians in the hospitals which I visited and I never heard one single complaint with regard to their treatment, or in respect to the medical, surgical or nursing services. On the contrary, they all spoke in the highest possible terms of the treatment which they have received in these hospitals. As I say, I think it unfortunate that this question of segregating should have arisen and to say the truth, I do not believe myself that Dr. Bruce had it in his mind that Canadian hospitals should he shut to all except Canadians. I think he had it in mind that a policy should be inaugurated that would aim at getting as many as possible of the Canadian soldiers in to Canadian hospitals. In my view as has so often happened in the case of these controversies, the truth lies between the two extremes. I know that that is the opinion of Sir George Parley, and that is the policy now being adopted. Instead of sending two, three, or half a dozen Canadians to a distance in Great Britain, they will, wherever possible, be sent to Canadian hospitals. So then we shall have a situation in which, in a hospital say of 1,000 beds we may have 300 or 400 or 500 or 700 Canadians, and the remainder British or Australians or New Zealand soldiers. As I 
say, there was a controversy in London with regard to this question. Lady Drummond had taken up the matter in the Times newspaper, and I desire to say with regard to Lady Drummond and the other ladies whom I saw in London, that they have laid this country under a debt of gratitude for the unselfish service which they have rendered to our soldiers.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Lady Drummond has maintained, 1 believe at her own expense, an establishment in London through which she is in communication with practically every Canadian soldier in Great Britain. That is a great service. I found the same with regard to other Canadian ladies in London. I do not believe we can speak too strongly or too highly of the service which these noble women are rendering in the cause of humanity there in London. I do not know anything that fills me with greater pride than the work being done by Canadian women in London and Great Britain.
There was the tension then that arose by reason of the feeling widely held that Dr. Bruce's report had not taken sufficiently into consideration the difficulties with which Surgeon General Jones had to contend, and that it did not do Surgeon General Jones the justice which it was thought by* the Canadian forces he was entitled to. There was also the tension caused by the controversy over the question of segregation which I have discussed. Then there was further question, and this was a most important matter, that .many members of the Canadian Medical Service and a good many of the leading officers of Great Britain, did not believe that Dr. Bruee's recommendations could be earned out practically. They did not believe that, having regard to conditions that existed at the front, and at the base hospitals, and the mode of transporting the casualties to the hospitals, that Dr. Bruce's recommendations could he carried out. That is to say they did not regard them as practicable. I talked with Dr. Bruce on one or two occasions in London, and I desire to be absolutely fair to him. As I say, he is a personal friend of mine. He is a surgeon of high standing, and in my view there are many excellent points in his report; but I do think that 'some of the recommendations which he made were impracticable, and I believe that the carrying out of them in their entirety or in large measure would have gone far to disorganize the Canadian Medi-

cal Service in Great Britain and on the continent.
Was he not promoted by the British War Office?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am not touching on Dr. Bruce's technical skill except to say that it is of a very high order. Dr. Bruce is the head of one of the services of the Toronto General Hospital. He is an associate professor of the University of Toronto, and I speak in the highest terms of his ability as a surgeon. What I am saying is that an opinion widely prevailed in military circles in Great Britain that it was not practicable to carry into effect many of Dr. Bruce's recommendations made in absolutely good faith-there is no question about that. That was the situation with which Sir George Perley was con-rfronted, and it was a .serious situation.

At what time was
that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
In November. It
was a serious situation, and it had. to be faced. Sir George Perley was obliged to act. This matter was given the best consideration of which we were capable. We reached the conclusion that in order to resolve the difficulties-because there was a clear cleavage of opinion, military and medical-we should have to appoint a board of inquiry in whom the people of Great Britain, including our own military men there, officers and men, and the people of Canada would have * complete confidence. I know that the selection of the personnel was approached in that spirit, and in that spirit only, because I myself advised with regard to some of the appointments. We thought it advisable to have a representative of the University of Toronto, a representative of Queen's University, Kingston, and a representative of McGill. The idea was to get a representative board in whom our military men, both officers and troops in Great Britain, would have confidence, and in whom the people of Canada would have confidence. Let us see whom we chose. I do not believe that a better or fairer board could by any possibility have been selected than that presided over by Dr. Baptie.

To-day I learned for the first time of those other medical men who were associated with Dr. Bruce. I assume that the minister's statement is accurate in regard to the other men, and that they assume responsibility for his statement.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think the position is this, that Dr. Bruce made the report, but I believe that some of these other gentlemen assisted him, obtained information for him, and reported to him. Dr. McKeown is a surgeon of high standing, who is connected with St. Michael's Hospital in Toronto. Dr. Wallace Scott is another physician of good standing connected with St. Michael's Hospital in Toronto. I say nothing against the ability of those men; they are well qualified surgeons,
Was the direction given to Dr. Bruce merely or to these gentlemen associated with him?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: To Dr. Bruce.
But they joined in the report?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not know that they joined in the report, but I think that Dr. Bruce made use of their services for the purpose of obtaining information, and no doubt embodied some of their conclusions or findings in his report.
Is it not rather humiliating to think that Dr. Bruce, a man of outstanding ability, having been ordered to investigate, should, after that, have been succeeded by another board to investigate him?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am explaining the circumstances which made the appointment of that board absolutely imperative if the Canadian medical service was not to be disorganized. I have explained all the circumstances which prevailed when the board was appointed. The board had to be appointed in order to deal with the acute differences which had arisen, and I want to refer for a moment now to the personnel of this board. I say that if the Government had tried for six months they could not have obtained better names than were obtained for the board which went into this matter at the instance of Sir George Perley and the Government in order to make a report for the purpose of settling these differences which had arisen, to ascertain whether these findings were correct and practicable. Who are the men of that commission? Who is Dr. Fotheringham? He is associate professor of medicine in the University of Toronto.

Nobody questions
that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Dr. Fotherdngham is on one of the medical services of Toronto General Hospital. Dr. Fothering-ham is a consulting physician of the highest standing an the city of Toronto. He is a man who has 'been connected for twenty or thirty years with the militia of Canada, a man of the highest possible standing. You could not select a physician in Toronto to-day who has in greater measure the confidence of the people of that city than has Dr. Fotheringham. So that no question arises as to him. Who is the other? Dr. Ross, of Kingston. The standing of Dr. Ross of Kingston is of the highest. He is a splendid man, a man who has the confidence of the people of Kingston and of Central Ontario, and I believe of most of the members of this House. Who else? Dr. Elder, of Montreal. Hon. gentlemen from Montreal will know him. No one can impeach his standing. I had the pleasure of conversing with Dr. Elder going over from Boulogne to. Folkestone. He is the leading surgeon, I believe, at the McGill Hospital at Folkestone, one of the best, if not the greatest hospital that this war has produced. He is the leading surgeon there, and does any one suppose that he would join in a report in which, he did not believe? Does any one suppose that Dr. Elder would make a report with regard to the question of Canadian wounded for any ulterior purpose Is there any hon. mem'beT who -will raise that question against Dr. Elder?
No one is raising a question against Dr. Bruce.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am contending that the men on this commission were men of the highest standing.
No one is questioning that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The ex-Minister of Militia has spoken, and spoken quite properly, in high terms of General Ashton. Then there was Sir William Baptie.

Does my hon. friend
think or say that the men on the Baptie Commission, were any better than Dr. Bruce and the men. who were working with him?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
At the outset oi my remarks I paid as high a tribute as I could to the surgical ability and standing of Dr. Bruce. I said that I had been on an hospital board long enough to know that

doctors differ and honestly differ. If I should have any criticism to make of Dr. Bruce, who is a personal friend of my own, it would not be on the ground of any lack of surgical skill, but on the ground that he had not the military experience which some of the men on that Commission had. I have a high opinion of Dr. Bruce's capabilities, and I said at the outset, and I sa>
now, that he made his report under instructions from the Minister and acted in all good faith.
Then we .have Sir William Baptie recommended to Sir George Perley by the British medical authorities. No one can challenge his standing. What happened? We have a report upon a report. We have Dr. Bruce's report, and we have a report on Dr. Bruce's report by five of the ablest medical men that could be selected.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: We have not the reports; that is the trouble.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Well, we are talking about them.
We cannot talk about them until we see them.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Then why are we discussing them? The reports have been made, and I am relating the circumstances under which they were made. Let us look for a moment at the V. A. D. question. I desire to say that Canada is under a debt of gratitude to those women who work late and early without regard to hours in connection with these hospitals. Why did the British authorities utilize these V. A. D. hospitals? It was for this reason, that they have had casualties on a scale undreamt ot a year ago. How many beds are in those V. A. D. hospitals? There are 53,000 beds, equivalent to 53 hospitals. The British medical authorities would tell you: "why of course we would rather have military hospitals, but we have to do the best we can, having regard to the exigencies of a situation in which casualties are coming by the tens of thousands when we expected them by the hundreds." They are only too glad to make use of these V. A. D. hospitals with 53,000 beds because they have not sufficient hospital accommodation otherwise. These are the facts.
So far as the Baptie .Commission is concerned, I have indicated the condition that existed in London, the controversy in regard to segregation and the strong feeling that was prevalent in the Canadian medical service in connection with the propos-

als to carry out the recommendations of Dr. Bruce's report. I have told the House the reasons (which .influenced Sir George Perley in appointing the Baptie Board of Inquiry. I have also informed the House, although most of us are aware, of the high standing of the members of that board. Until the two reports are tabled, it is quite impossible for the House to form its conclusion upon them, but I desire to say that from numerous conversations which I had with men, with officers, with members of the Canadian medical service, with distinguished medical practitioners in London, and with other prominent people there, I am absolutely of the opinion that in no war in the history of the wprld has there been anything like the high excellence of medical treatment of the soldiers as has been given to the troops of Great Britain and the Dominions overseas in this war. I desire to say this further, that of the hundreds of men with whom I talked in the hospitals which I visited, Canadian soldiers and Canadian nurses, from almost every constituency represented in this House, all spoke in the highest possible terms of the medical and surgical treatment and of the nursing which has been furnished to the wounded, and I came away with a feeling that all was well in connection with the treatment which had been accorded our Canadian soldiers in Great Britain. Further than that,' the Canadian soldiers in Great Britain, while they desire to see a large representation of Canadians in the hospitals, in so far as I was able to gather their opinipn from conversation, and from hundreds of letters from Canadian soldiers, do not desire segregation. They do not desire that Canadian hospitals should be maintained exclusively for Canadian soldiers. They want a percentage, a large representation, but they certainly do not desire the doors ,of the hospital to be closed to the soldiers from New Zealand, Australia, Scotland, England or Ireland. They want to talk with these men. They find it interesting to talk with them. I believe that the association of our wounded soldiers with the wpunded soldiers from Australia and New Zealand and other parts of the British Empire will make greatly for the promotion of Imperial sentiment.

Will this lying alongside of an Australian or a New Zealander in a hospital impart any more of the Imperial spirit to the heart or the soul of a man whose loyalty was staunch enough to impel him to fight for the Empire.
35i

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: All these influences contribute to the development of Imperial spirit. There is a comradeship which they greatly value. I never saw a soldier who intimated a contrary opinion. They value the comradeship of the men from the British Isles from New Zealand and Australia. They value the comradeship of their own fellow Canadians and they want to be with them but they do not desire that the Canadian hospitals should be wholly for Canadians. I do not wish to labour that point. I repeat, what I said a few moments ago, that the truth in regard to this matter, as it does in so many cases, lies between the two extremes. On the one hand, I think it is a mistake to send Canadians in small groups to remote parte of the United Kingdom, but, on the other hand, I do not believe that Canadian hospitals should be solely for Canadian wounded. You might have a Canadian hospital with a thousand beds and five or six hundred Canadians in it. Are you going to say that the unoccupied beds shall not be available for wounded soldiers from England, New Zealand or Australia?
Does Dr. Bruce say that? *

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No,, he does not say that. I said before the ex-Minister of Militia came in that I did not believe Dr. Bruce had that in mind. I said that the policy which I understood him to put forward was that we should, as far as possible, have our Canadian soldiers in the Canadian hospitals. I think it is unfortunate that this " segration " controversy should have arisen in London. I know that Sir George Perley's view is that the truth lies between the two extremes and I think the matter is now satisfactorily adjusted.

I understand that there were two commissions, and each commission, I presume, made recommendations. Will the minister tell me if there was anything done to implement any of the recommendations made by either commission?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I understand
from the Prime Minister, who has had the matter more immediately in charge, that the recommendations of the Baptie Commission are being carried out.
Wherein did the recommendations of the Baptie Commission differ from the recommendations of Colonel Bruce's Commission?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not propose to go into the details of Dr. Bruce's report. The ex-minister was absent during the major part of my remarks this afternoon. I stated among other things that some of the recommendations made by Dr. Bruce were, in the view of the military authorities, impracticable. With reference to the details of the Baptie report, as the matter is not particularly under the jurisdiction of my department, I do not propose to enter into it. I have taken up the time of the House this afternoon because I think it would be unfortunate in the last degree if the impression should be created erroneously in this country that Canadian wounded are not receiving proper treatment in Great Britain. I believe they are. I believe they have been well treated, that they have had the benefit of the highest medical skill and the best nursing possible, and I have never heard a contrary opinion put forward by any soldier or officer either here or in Great Britain.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Except by Colonel Bruce.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am speaking of the men with whom I talked.
Was Dr. Bruce's promotion recommended by Sir George Perley to the War Office?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I understand it was the British service that he was recently appointed to, although I am not informed as to the truth of the report to that effect.
On whose recommendation?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There was a newspaper report that Dr. Bruce was to enter the Imperial service to act in the capacity of consulting surgeon in France. I should imagine that Dr. Bruce would be highly qualified for a position of that kind.
Is it not extraordinary, after his having been taken to task by Dr. Baptie, that he should be promoted by the Imperial authorities?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not think there is anything extraordinary about it. If my hon. friend has had as much experience of physicians and surgeons as I have had, he will know that they differ and honestly differ. You frequently have men of the highest standing and ability who differ, but that does not mean that they are unqualified in their profession. My opinion is that Dr.

Bruce would make an excellent consulting surgeon.
