I observed in the report which purported to be issued by the Baptie Commission that an " if " came in; that so long as it was decided that the Canadians and the British land others should mix together they did not think they should be segregated. If I remember aright, this report contained a condition that " if " it was decided to keep the Canadians, Australians, and British soldiers together, then they would agree with Dr. Bruce's report, but otherwise they would not agree.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have no information as to that.

It has been reported that my hon. friend from West Lam'bton (Mr. Pardee) made a statement that a soldier who was returning from the front by the name of Private G. Walton, of Windsor, invalided home-
-was without overcoat or gloves, and had his hands frozen at Quebec. He is being cared for in the London hospital, and his case should receive such attention as will make similar cases impossible.
Then the hon. gentleman continues:-
That is one concrete case, and, I have no doubt, there are hundreds of similar cases.
I desire to say to my hon. friend that, in regard to this statement, I have received the following telegram:-
Windsor, Ont., Peb. 6, 1917.
O. J. Wilcox,
House of Commons.
Re Pardee newspaper story, Private G. Walton frozen hands account; no issue coats and mitts absolutely false; was met by Sportsman Patriotic Assistant Secretary. Writing particulars.
M. G. Campbell,
President.
I simply allude to this fact to show how careful hon. gentlemen ought to be in reading these newspaper trashy reports as actual proof of conditions.
Mr. PARDEE; I simply told the House that I was reading from a newspaper. I did not take it upon myself to say whether it was true or not; I was simply pointing it out.
At six o'clock, the Committee took recess.
After Recess.
The committee resumed at eight o'clock. -Mr. Blain in the Chair.

On section 2-payment of $500,000,000 may be made.

speakeroldname: Mr. D. D. McKENZIE (North Cape Breton) :
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I realize that it is desirable to make any observations that I have to make on this Bill as brief as possible. I did intend to speak upon the resolution; but time did not permit last night, and it was agreed, I understand, that the same discussion could be carried on in committee on the Bill. The field for discussion which this large vote opens up is very inviting, and my sole purpose in addressing you, Sir, at this juncture is to discharge what I regard as a serious duty to my own constituents, in explaining to them the salient points of this Bill. The Bill itself in a concise way sets forth its purpose. It involves the voting of an enormous sum of money, I suppose the largest individual vote that has ever been before the Parliament of Canada; at all events the largest within my memory of any transactions of this kind in this House. The preamble of the Bill says-
Whereas a state of war exists between His Majesty and the German Emperor, the Emperor of Austria, King of Hungary, the Sultan of Turkey, and the King of the Bulgarians; and whereas it is necessary that measures be taken for the common defence and security, and to this end it is expedient that aid as hereinafter provided be rendered to His Majesty: Therefore His Majesty, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate and House of Commons of Canada, enacts as follows:-
The second section of the Bill, which is
the important one, says:
From and out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund there may be paid and applied beyond the ordinary grants of Parliament a sum not exceeding five hundred million dollars towards defraying any expenses that may be incurred by or under the authority of the Governor in Council during the year ending the thirty-first day of March, 1918.
It is important for the people of this country to have some understanding as to what is to be done with this enormous sum of money. The subdivisions of section 2 set out what those different matters are, and as they are all highly important, I desire to refer to them for a few moments. They are:
(a)	the defence and security of Canada;
(b)	the conduct of naval and military operations in or beyond Canada;
(c)	promoting the continuance of trade, industry, and business communications, whether by means of insurance or indemnity against war risk or otherwise;
(d)	the carrying out of any measures deemed necessary or advisable by the Governor in Council in consequence of the existence of a state of war; and
(e)	payments made for the said purposes during the fiscal year ending the thirty-first day of March, nineteen hundred and seventeen, in excess of the amount authorized by The War Appropriation Act, 1916.
Speaking for my people, I am not finding fault with this vote; far from it. I am heartily in accord with it, and the only advice which I would attempt to submit would be that the money should be applied carefully and properly to the different subjects enumerated in subsection 2 of this Bill. Liberal as I am, and a true follower of a great Liberal leader, I could not be anything other than in entire accord with proper expenditure being made and proper steps being taken by this Parliament and this country in support of the position which we have so proudly taken in this war. Some attempts are being made in certain quarters to show that the Liberal leader and those who follow him are not doing as much as they ought to; that they are not sincere in their support of the Government in war conditions, and, in fact, that the leader of this great party is not in favour of participation in the wars of Great Britain at all. I was particularly struck by an article which appeared a few days ago in a Conservative paper published in the province of Quebec. La Patrie, I understand, is a stout advocate of Tory principles, a paper which is edited by bright, capable, business young men who understand the politics of this country and who are familiar with the history of the different political parties. I feel gratified that they take a proper view of the position of the great Liberal leader in connection with military matters in the Dominion of Canada, and of his judgment and of the judgment of his party in regard to the relations which Canada should have with matters political and matters imperial in the old land. I think it was about the 25th of January last, when party politics in the province of Quebec were at a high temperature, that La Patrie tried to find fault with my great leader and to hold him up as a man who was not in line with the ideas of the Conservative party, because this paper said:
If Sir Wilfrid Laurier were in power should we participate in the present war? Certainly. It was Sir Wilfrid Laurier who first defined! this policy of participation In 1897 at the Jubilee of Queen Victoria in London. "When the hour of battle strikes," he said, "light your beacon-fires on the hills, sound your trumpets and Canada will answer your call in sacrificing the best of her blood.''
In 1899 for the first time the Canadian Government took part in an Empire war. The

Laurier Government sent the contingent to Africa.
In 1910 Laurier brought about the adoption of the Navy Bill, affirming this constitutional truth:	"When Britain (England) is at war,
Canada is at war." This navy should be Canadian in peace time and Imperial in war time.
It is Sir Wilfrid Laurier who is the sponsor of military Imperialism in Canada.
That is the position taken by the leader whom I am proud to follow, and it is represented in La Patrie, which intended to put this statement forward as an offence to my great leader and- as something which would not be acceptable to the Conservative party in the province of Quebec, particularly in regard to the election going on in the county of Dorchester, and this particular quotation was published for the purpose of rendering matters difficult for the, candidate of Sir Wilfrid Laurier in that constituency. I say, therefore, that the expenditure of this money, if it is properly expended in support of King and country in connection with the situation in which we find ourselves, is perfectly satisfactory to me as a humble follower of my great leader.
We had an opportunity of hearing eloquent discussions upon the various phases of the management of the war since it commenced down to the present hour, but we did not hear anything from the Treasury benches that would strengthen our confidence in the manner in which war appropriations have been spent in the past I am sorry that in this discussion no evidence has been given either by the Minister of Militia (Mr. Kemp) or the Secretary for War (Mr. McCurdy)-if that be the proper title-of ability or willingness to explain the matters placed in their charge. One Minister of Militia has been dismissed. One would naturally suppose that the reason for that dismissal is that the Prime Minister thought he had not sufficient grasp of the affairs of his department, especially in view of the tremendous responsibility we have undertaken in participating in this desperate struggle now going on in Europe. And in selecting a man to take the place of the Minister whom he dismisses, one would suppose that the Prime Minister, especially as he has such a wide clientele, so to speak, from which to select, would choose a man having at least a fair knowledge of the subject in hand, and ability to give to the House a business presentment of how the money voted by Parliament had been spent, and a reasonable explanation of the plans of proposed expenditure. I have no fault to find personally with the hon. member who has been selected to be

Minister of Militia. I have sat in this House with him for some years and have always found him a genial gentleman. But I had hoped that when the House met this year he would show some knowledge of the business for which he was selected, and would give a business account of what is being done by the department. I know that the gentleman appointed as Secretary for War-still assuming that to be the proper title-is a business man, and I expected that he would give some business idea of what was being done both upon this side and upon the other side of the water. But to my amazement-and I speak sincerely-I find thait both the minister and his lieutenant are as dumb as oysters, and, assuming that they know anything about the affairs in their charge, refuse to share with us their store of knowledge. It does not require great eloquence to give the House a business idea of what expenditures have been made and what the plans for future expenditure in connection with this war may be. It surely is a surpiising thing that it should be thought necessary to have a special pleader in the person of the Solicitor General to tell this House what is being done. To me it is always an indication that things are not what they ought to be when the Solicitor General is called in to give a statement to the House-one, as the Shakespearean phrase has it to make the worse appear the better reason. I do not now find fault with the way in which the Solicitor General puts the case; what I say is that it is not his case, it is not his business. A few years ago, we in this country were putting through a big transaction in the Transcontinental railway, and we were scoffed at by the present Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden), then the leader of the Opposition, because, forsooth, we had lawyers on the Cofnmission. He said we had no business to have lawyers handling such matters. He must have changed his mind; because now, even when dealing with military matters; with the making of ammunition; with rifles, and differentiating between one rifle and another, or between one class of ammunition and another; with tactics on a battlefield; this House must pass over the Minister of Militia and the Secretary for War, and must pass over an ex-Minister of Militia as well, and learn from the Solicitor General what is being done in these matters. Surely the Prime Minister will remember how he used, to attack us for trusting to lawyers business that 'he said belonged to Parliament. I want to be honest with myself. Of men

who are not specialists in any business that is to be dealt with, the lawyer has as much opportunity of knowing about that business as anybody. For, if he has any practice in the courts, he has to deal with every kind of business, and, while, he is master of no trade, he will know something about a great many.
We are called upon to hand over this huge sum of money to the Governor in Council. Well, we all know who the Governor in Council are. But will any of these hon. gentlemen sitting on the Treasury benches say that he knows anything about war matters? I do not think there is one of them who would venture to cast the first stone at the ex-Minister of Militia (Sir Sam Hughes) if the accusation were that that horn gentleman did not know enough about military affairs. There is the Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White). He is a splendid speaker. But because a man is a good speaker it does not follow that he is a good financier or a good business man. If I had any advice to give the hon. Minister of Finance, it would be to pay less attention to the rules of elocution and more to the multiplication table. If I have any weakness about the Minister of Finance it is in thinking too much of him. I suppose that I still have some of the old regard that men always feel for an erring brother, based, I suppose, on the! hope that he will complete the circle and some day find his way back to the Liberal fold. Perhaps the Minister of Finance is too easily dissuaded from his purposes. I think it was on the evening of the 30th of last month that the hon. gentleman was speaking when the House rose at six o'clock. At that time he was going strong in a certain direction and talking pretty straight about the exMinister of Militia and his manoeuvring in his department.
When he came back after dinner, he saw a great light. Our- Saul of Tarsus had become Paul the Apostle, and he had little, if anything, to say against the manipulations of the ex-Minister of Militia. I have a third quotation here, the words of which clearly indicate that they were uttered after dinner. I am .not now suggesting that a dinner in Ottawa means very much, or that any reason of that kind resulted in a changed view on the part of the Minister of Finance. However, when he came back he said:
I repeat that if you take all the nations that are engaged in this war, and have regard to the scale of their operations, the mode of purchase, the administrative acts which have been
taken, their financial operations, having regard also to the proportion which must be observed between their operations and ours, in my belief there has been less waste in connection with the administration of the Militia Department and this Government of Canada than in connection with the administration of any other belligerent in the world. I say that not only with regard to the present war but in regard to any war of the past.
That is a most extraordinary statement for the minister to make. The Minister of Finance never went through a war before this one, and I never heard of any book being published which made comparative statements respecting wastefulness in matters connected with war. I am at a loss, therefore, to know how my hon. friend is in a position to say that the conditions prevailing in Canada since the war began have been economically superior to anything that has ever happened since the world began. One would hardly suppose that a careful, cool, calculating mathematician such as the Minister of Finance ought to be would make statements of that kind without having the very best proof to back them up. This statement was made by the Minister of Finance after (the ex-Minister of Militia had spoken on the same evening, and no doubt it was with the statement of his expert in mind that the Minister of Finance made this declaration of economy. If hon. gentlemen will refer to Hansard of January 30, page 279, they will find the following:
Mr. Pugsley:	Before my hon. friend leaves
that matter, could' he say what was the value of the equipment which was thrown away?
Sir Sam Hughes:	X forget; it was millions.
We did not look at the value; we tvere so busy swearing.
That is the evidence upon which the Minister of Finance reached the conclusion that the greatest economy and thrift ever known had been practised-a declaration by the ex-minister that he could not look at figures, never knew anything about the multiplication table-he was too busy swearing. I should not care to go to a jury with evidence of that kind and ask them to give me a verdict according to the evidence. That, Sir, is one reason why I find fault with the Minister of Finance and one reason why I should hesitate, if the case were not as urgent as it is, to put $500,000,000 into his hands to be expended as may be deemed proper by him and those associated with liim-for I assume that the counsel of the Minister of Finance will have to prevail in matters affecting the disbursement of this money.
I had intended to quote a few gems from the speeches of the ex-Minister of War. I

realize that the ex-minister is not such an authority to-day with my friends opposite as he used to be. I have recollections of seeing during the last five years my distinguished friends across the way making most elaborate salaams to this dignitary, with palms in their hands. But now I observe that only one member on that side of the House pays the slightest attention to the ex-minister, and that is the hon. member for Chateauguay, a gentleman who, I understand, is engaged in the business of manufacturing and selling tombstones. This is explained by the old saying: "Where the carcass is, there the eagles will gather". I want to give the Minister of Finance further evidence of the kind of economy that was practised during the five years that the ex-Minister of Militia was in office. I find that the ex-minister, as reported on page 511 of Hansard, after making some extensive observations regarding the wastefulness that he said was being practised on both sides of the water, says:
This is the way this humbug goes on, up and down.
He says further, on the same page:
There is no doubt that the world put two and two together. Nobody could know of the conspiracy in my department, and this was part and parcel of the conspiracy from start to finish. And yet these gentlemen are there to-day.
He intimates that while he was in office some men in the department evidently had nothing to do but conspire to defeat him in some of his purposes-laudable purposes, no doubt-and he says that those who were conspiring, are still there. That circumstance is not such as causes me to have great confidence in the administration of the Governor in Council. He says further, speaking about the kind of ammunition that was being made:
Yes, they are on record.
That is, the nature of the different kinds of ammunition.
The three brands were defective and no rifle could have fired them. One of them was so deadly that to have sent men to the firing line with it would have been simply murder. We found an ordnance officer attached to Canadian headquarters issuing that ammunition to the extent of 5,000 rounds which were placed in the pouches of one battalion after the blow-up. X have no hesitation in saying that that ordnance officer should have been led out and shot, and if I had been running the show I would have carried that out. I protested, and demanded his dismissal, but he is there yet.
What does he mean by calling it a show?

I do not know, perhaps a sort of zoo he was running, but I do not know what he means by it. I't seems there were some parties concerned in the show who did not dance to his pipe, and he certainly finds fault. But this is too serious for me to pass over without calling the Prime Minister's attention to it. There is somebody somewhere for whom the Prime Minister is responsible who was putting ammunition in the pouches and bags of Canadian soldiers, and the giving of that ammunition to them was, according to the ex-minister, equivalent to murder. That is a very serious matter, and I heard no explanation and no contradiction by the Prime Minister, or the Minister of Militia, or tlhe Secretary of War; they have allowed this to go by the board and made no explanation of it at all. If I should be asked by my constituents: Have you consented to giving $500,000,000 to that group of gentlemen to be expended by them? Did you find out if that sort of officer is yet in dbarge? Is that same officer, */ho, according to the ex-Minister of Militia, should have been shot, and who he says is still in the employ of the Government, is he yet there and is he still going to have charge of the ammunition to be given to our boys to defend themselves? I cannot say. The hon. gentlemen on the other side iare not very communicative. They will not tell us. But this is what the ex-Minister of Militia has said, and we have no reason to suppose that he has said anything but the truth.
He gave us another pathetic statement about the Highland Brigade, and he disclosed the truth, which is really pathetic, about the condition of things which existed in the camp. A good deal of fault has been found in the province from which I come in respect to that Highland Brigade. It was promised, as the ex-minister has said, that these men would be kept together. He says that he bad the authority of the Prime Minister in making that statement. On the strength of that statement the very best men that we have in the province of Nova Scotia went out recruiting. I may mention as one Bishop . Morrison, of the diocese of Antigonish. Bishop Morrison went out among his people with this promise in his hand, that young men would be kept together, that they would not be broken up, that brothers, relatives, neighbours would be together and it would be a sort of outing for them where they would not be separated. On the strength of that promise he got many Scotch Highland Cath-

dies in Antigonish and all through his diocese to join. What will Bishop Morrison say to-day to the fathers and mothers who come to him and say: Bishop, you promised our boys would be kept together; we took your word for it, and they went out; but now we find that they are broken up, sent hither and thither, and there is no unity in the regiments as you promised. I think the Prime Minister should have some regard for the obligations and the feelings of gentlemen of that class who went forth believing the Government would do what they promised to do and represented to the people that that would be the case; and that certainly the word of the Government, as presented by the Prime Minister, would not be departed from. I am sure that for myself I should be quite willing to take the Prime Minister's word for such a statement, as for almost anything else; but 1 -am sorry to say that his residence in Ontario and -his commingling with such people as he associates with does not help him along the lines of stability and veracity. What the ex-Minister of Militia said is this:
When the Highland Brigade of Nova Scotia was organized I felt a little keen in regard to the matter because of what had happened and I took the matter up with the Prime Minister. With his authority I gave my solemn pledge! to the officers of the brigade and to the committee that had helped to organize it that it would be kept intact. The Prime Minister may recall that on one occasion he spoke to me about the 58th Battalion. I said, "for heaven's sake let us carry out one pledge which we have made to the people of Nova Scotia.''
It was, of course, very pathethic. The ex-minister -says: "everything else has gone; we have made thousands of pledges, we have broken them, they are gone, but this one thing, stand by the pledge that you and I gave to the people of Nova Scotia". But no, they did not stand by it, it is gone.
The ex-minister comes to the question of financing again. He calls to account the Prime Minister and others for their system of financing the brigades, and he says that there were more men drilled at Camp Borden, Camp Valcartier and elsewhere in Canada than are -being drilled on the other side. Then he says:
Why all this paraphernalia should be introduced in London X have never been able to find out.
The Prime Minister is familiar with our Statutes in Nova Scotia, and he knows that our Probate Act refers to paraphernali i. Paraphernalia is something that is never considered worth mentioning in an inventory and although it is the property of the
dead man there is nothing said about it. I do not know whether that is the -sort of paraphernalia that the Minister refers to here. However, he does not give any description of it beyond the statement that there is a paraphernalia and that paraphernalia exists in London. He says:
General Carson, with Colonel George Murphy, and thirty-one assistants, ran the business-
That is during his regime.
-and when any hon. gentleman asked for any news of his friends at the front he got an answer within a few days. When any hon. gentleman asked if any one was wounded or wanted a report about any one, he got his answer in a very few days from General Carson. To-day you get nothing. General Carson with only thirty-one officers could keep the work going, train men, and send- them to the front and win battles, whereas to-day I am told there are 700 assistants, costing $6,000,000 a year, as the result of the action of the Minister of Finance when he ordered the Prime Minister to appoint an overseas minister ; I forget what he was going to do. We find all that saddled on the country, and I presume to-night the Minister of Finance is preaching thrift and economy to the people of Ottawa.
He is, on one hand, squandering the money of the people of Canada, and in his line of talk going around preaching economy. That is what his colleague or the man who was his colleague for the last five years accuses him of. That, sir, to some extent is the testimony u,pon which the decision of the Minister of Finance is based when he tells this country that there never was in this world (or almost in the world to come) any such high-class economy as was practised in Canada. I find here a letter from the ex-Minister of Mi-litia to the Prime Minister bearing date 13th of May, 1915, which was put on record by himself I am going to quote only a few lines from it. He said:
I wrote a letter to the Prime Minister on May 13, and X presume there is no objection to my reading it. The faults complained in it have been rectified by the War Purchasing Commission, and I think it is in justice to myself that I should place it on record to show the life we had to lead in the Militia Department :
May 13, 1915.
Dear Sir Robert,
Since my return from England last November, I have repeatedly notified you that owing to the interference and plans of the " so-called " sub-committee and to the repeated hold-ups and needless obstructions of some of my colleagues in the affairs' of this department, the Contract Branch has been very much hampered and practically blockaded; delays have been very prolonged ; the cost has been greatly enhanced and the goods supplied have been, in many cases, inferior. Indeed, the most ardent agents of the German Government-

This is the part to which I desire to call the attention of the Prime Minister particularly :

indeed the most ardent agents of the German Government could scarcely have been more successful in holding up the proper equipment of our forces, had they been in control.
That, Sir, is a tremendous indictment. We are told by the ex-Minister of Militia that even if the most ardent agents of our arch enemy had been in charge of matters in the Militia Department and of the Government, they could not have been more successful in obstructing and blocking our success than those who were in charge. That goes without a reply. It is not for me to say it is not true. I believe if it was not true it would have been contradicted. I notice that the special pleader, the learned counsel, who comes forward to save the ship when there are rocks and breakers in sight, steered clear of this piece of dangerous and hazardous navigation. He did not tell us anything about that. I will be asked by my constituents: were you a party to handing over to the Government $500,000,000, and I will have to admit that I was. I consent to it because, for the present, they are the only power. I will have to plead theology, and say that the power is from the Lord, although the party in power are rather poor representatives in exercising it sometimes. But I will have to say that for the present they are the power, and d will, have to plead my theological knowledge in voting them the money in the hope that they will do better things, and that no minister, or any other man who may have inside knowledge of the working of this Government, will ever again be in a position to say that this Government, or a certain wing of it, was more successful in blocking the preparations of war than any agency of the Germans could have been if they had had the matter in hand. I trust that the outgoing of the Minister of Militia (Sir Sam Hughes) will have the effect of stirring up the Prime Minister and those who support him, and of ensuring that matters will be better handled in the future than they have been in the past.
If we were to go upon the evidence, and if the occasion would permit us to cause any delay in granting the money, I would feel justified in supporting that delay and stopping the supply if that were possible. But the matter is too urgent, and the occasion is too grave and I am sure that the people who sent me here would rather take the grave risks of having the money spent,

perhaps recklessly and ineffectively in some regards, than have me for one moment interfere with the voting of the money. I am sure there are many people in my riding who will regard this expenditure as very large. As I said at the beginning it is, so far as I know, the largest vote that ever came before a Canadian Parliament. It involves the payment of $62.50 by every man, woman and child in the Dominion of Canada, and of $312.50 for every family of five in the Dominion. These are large amounts, but still the cause is worthy, and we are heart and soul behind this thing. We can only hope that we shall get proper value for the expenditure of the money. There must be a landmark from which the Prime Minister can start afresh, turn a new page; and if he cannot turn a new page in everything, he can surely turn a new page in regard to the question of patronage. This is an opportunity for him to start a fresh page in the matter of patronage. I am speaking only about the province of Nova Scotia, for I know very little of what is being done elsewhere. I have told the Prime Minister over and over again, and I take the responsibility of telling him again, that there is not the slightest difference between the expenditure of war money, so far as patronage is concerned, and the expenditure of any other vote that passes this House. It is well known that in the Department of Marine and Fisheries, in the Department of Public Works, and in the Department of the Interior, though they have not very much patronage in the Department of the Interior, the expenditure is strictly along party lines and is distributed among party friends and party favourites. I take the responsibility of saying, and I challenge contradiction from any member of this House, or from any one outside of this House, to say that in the province from which I come there is the slightest difference between the expenditure of war moneys that we vote in this way, and other moneys that are voted. I submit to the Prime Minister that this would be a good occasion for him to make a fresh resolution to start anew and spend this money in such a way that nobody can find fault and so that Grit and Tory, saint and sinner, shall have an equal opportunity of giving value for the money which has to be expended.
I have not very much more to say in connection with this matter. I hope that we shall get good returns for this very large expenditure, and that those whom the

Prime Minister has called to his council, his Minister of Militia, and his Secretary of War, will take this matter in hand and try to learn something about it. So far, they have not given us the slightest evidence that they knew anything about it at all, and I think it is a pity that we should be called upon to pay handsome salaries to ministers and their secretaries, when we have not the slightest evidence that they are taking any interest in the matter, but, on the contrary, are leaving it entirely to parties outside. I presume we should not expect very much from them this session, but when we meet again after the adjournment I hope that they will have learned' something about their departments, and about this business, and that when questions are asked concerning matters pertaining particularly to the War Department we shall get an answer first-hand from the proper source, and not have to take it second-hand from people who. are not supposed to know very much about it, and who try to cover up the crevices of their ignorance by the continuous flow of their eloquence.
Before I sit ddwn, I wish to call the attention of the Minister of Militia to a case that has been brought to my attention concerning a soldier who enlisted at Windsor, in the province of Nova Scotia. A young man by the name of H. Bruce Hawkins was enlisted by Lieutenant Fielding at Windsor on the 25th September, 1916. He was examined by Dr. Keddy-I presume of Windsor-and passed tihe examination. Lieutenant Fielding told him that his pay would begin on the day that he was passed by Dr. Keddy. On the 4th October, 1916, he was given transportation to St. John, N.B., on arrival there was examined by a board of examiners, and directed, after he had passed the examination, to join the company of Lieutenant Blair. From there he went to Montreal. Arriving at Montreal, he was again examined by a medical board, passed and put on duty. When pay day arrived he was not paid and the paymaster had no record of his joining the company. He was told that he had been reported by Lieutenant Blair as being in the St. John hospital. That is an extraordinary condition of things. Lieutenant Blair took him to Montreal, passed him over to some other officer and then reported that he was in the hospital in St. John. It was about the 24th October, 1916, that this young man went looking for his pay. Then he was reexamined by a board of examiners who found that there was a small piece of his
little finger that was slightly touching on the third1 finger and for that reason he was discharged and sent back with no clothing except what he had when he left home and without a cent of money. I am informed that he was obliged to pawn his watch in Montreal with a man by the name of Heller, at 217 St. Lawrence street. Hon. gentlemen from Montreal will know whether I am giving a true account or not. Mr. Heller took his watch in security for a little money to take him home. He was obliged to go back home and was not paid for the month or more that he was in the service. He had passed the medical examination three times-first by Dr. Keddy, then by the board at St. John, and then by the board at Montreal. He did everything he could do to enlist, but from the time that he offered himself to the present he has not been paid anything. I just want to draw this to the attention of the right hon. the Prime Minister and the hon. Minister of Militia in the hope that they will take some steps to do justice to this poor young man and see that he gets the little money that is coming to him for the time during which he served. This information was sent to me iand I was asked to- bring it to the notice of the minister. I have done so in this way, because, the time being short, I have had no opportunity of calling upon the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: Will my hon. friend be good enough to give the name of the battalion in which he enlisted so that we can trace it in that way?

I may be able to get that information, but I do not have it in my hands at the present moment. That is all I have to say on that matter . In conclusion, let me express the hope that wise counsels will prevail across the way, that this bickering and fighting, now that the ex-Minister of Militia has gone, will pass away and that we will learn that there are other people in the world who can do something besides the hon. gentleman who has left the Cabinet. Of course, in times of wiar, I suppose we will be disillusioned in a great many directions. For 4,000 years we have been under the delusion that the Lord had created the heavens and the earth, the firmament iand the waters under the earth. Now, we 'are all disillusioned, because we find that all these 'things were done by Sir Sam Hughes himself. However, we are learning and we hope that the Prime Minister and the rest of them have not lived in vain with this great man for the last five years.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
London, Jan. 31, 1917.
Statements that Canadian leather equipment has been burned on arrival in England are absurd and untrue. Oliver equipment with which First Division proceeded to France was subsequently replaced here without expense to Canadian public and it was returned to Canada early in 1915 for use there. Converted Oliver equipment with which Second Division was equipped was replaced before going to France and later returned to Canada for further service. 1916 Canadian leather equipment with which Fourth Division proceeded to France was eventually replaced by web equipment without expense to Canadian public. Large number of troops in training in England use Canadian leather equipment. Sufficient web equipment is now being supplied troops in training in England to enable reinforcements to proceed overseas with acceptable equipment properly adjusted.
It seemed to me desirable that I should make that statement to the committee.
With respect to certain other matters which have been raised, I might say that . the Second contingent was authorized: by order in council ot November 7, 1914. The despatch ot that contingent to England commenced on tlie 10th of April, 1915, and wiae completed on the 9th of August of that year. The number of ships required was twenty-one, and the total numbers that went forward in the contingent were: officers 930, other ranks 21,640, total 22,570. I am further informed, by memorandum placed in my hands by the Deputy Minister of Militia and Defence, that the contingent was rl spatdhed to England as soon as accommodation and transports were available. I am informed that this contingent went to the front on September 13, 1915.
I have already explained that the motor trucks with which this contingent was equipped were loaned for the time being from the War Office. I have here a memorandum on the purchase of these motor trucks which I desire to read:
The purchase of motor trucks was authorized by order in council dated 15th December, 1914 ; -50 trucks from the Kelly-Springfleld Company, Springfield, Ohio; 50 trucks from the Packard, Detroit, Michigan; and 50 trucks from the White Company, Cleveland, Ohio. One of the terms of the order in council was that if any of these firms failed to accept the order under the conditions named in the order in council, the portion of the order allotted to ' such firms should be distributed among the others accepting the conditions price: list price, less 20 per cent, discount f.o.b. place of manufacture. It was a further condition of the order that each firm representing any truck purchased should agree to have made in Canada such portions of the bodies and tire work as could be done in this country. Orders were placed in Canada by telegram for the bodies on 17th December, 1914, and for the tires on December 18th,	1914. The order for the
chassis was delayed owing to the desire of the

Prime Minister to institute certain inquiries in regard to the reliability of the Kelly-Springfield motor. On 5th January, 1915, the Prime Minister instructed to proceed with placing the order, and on the 15th of that month the firms named in the order in council were asked by wire to supply the trucks.
I interrupt the memorandum to say that a question had been raised as to the durability and reliability of the Kelly-Spring-field motor, and it seemed to me desirable that the doubt 'Should be absolutely cleared up before we should proceed to give an order. For that reason there was a delay during which I undertook to satisfy myself on ithatt point. It eventually proved thiait the motor was entirely .serviceable. The memorandum continues:
The Kelly-Springfield Company accepted immediately and the contract was made on the 16 th January. The White Company offered only twenty per cent, f.o.b. Cleveland, and the Packard Company did not close within the period specified for acceptance, viz.: one week. The balance of the order was accordingly given to the Kelly-Springfield Company, who completed the entire delivery of the chassis by 19th February. 1915.
My recollection of the exact terms of the order is that we insisted that the various companies from whom these motor trucks were to be purchased should give a price to the Government based on a deduction of the commission which they allowed to their agents. As we were ordering direct, we thought the Government was entitled to a deduction equal to the commission ordinarily paid. The memorandum proceeds:
Owing, however, to the bodies originally ordered not fitting, and fresh bodies having to be made, the motor trucks did not arrive in England in time to equip the Second Division. But the Second Division was not delayed in proceeding overseas or in going to France by reason thereof. The trucks for this division were borrowed from the War Office and replaced by our trucks on their arrival in England. The Government lost nothing by their exchange with the War Office, as the trucks supplied by Canada, while just as efficient as the Imperial, cost less money.
There is another matter upon which I desire to give the committee some information, as the question is raised by the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver). He spoke of the response to the National Service card. On the 2nd instant, I procured from the Secretary of the National Service Board a statement as to the number of cards which had been received up to that time. He informs me that the estimate of National Service cards received to that date was 1,350,220, and that the cards were still being received at the rate of about 40,000 per day.

The right hon. gentleman who leads the House has told us that there have been a lot of wrong statements regarding the scrapping of articles of war equipment purchased in Canada and taken overseas. So far as this House is concerned, the information that we get in this matter is from the ex-Minister of Militia (Sir Sam Hughes). He more than any one else has stated that articles purchased in this country have been scrapped. So, if anything has been wrongly stated, it comes from a former colleague of the right hon. Prime Minister. And I can hardly suppose that the ex-Minister of Militia has made such erroneous statements as would appear from the statements read by the Prime Minister. But that will be a question for investigation later on. At present, we are asked to appropriate $500,000,000 to be handed over to this Government to expend at their own sweet will. This is an amount which would have staggered the imagination of Canadians a few years ago -a very few years ago. To-day, we feel that we are strong enough financially to stand expenditure of this kind. But it is our duty, and the people of 'the country will see to it that we are held responsible for the performance of that duty, to see to it that this money is properly expended. There has been some discussion in the press of the formation of a national government. If anything would induce me to believe that the time was ripe for a national government, it would be the fact that we are asked to hand over $500,000,000 to the Government now in power. Consider the statements that have been made by ministers of the Crown themselves. Judging by what the ex-Minister of Militia has said, it would appear that for months, yes for years, he in his department was surrounded by what a former Prime Minister of Canada called, a nest of traitors. The Minister of Finance rises in his place in this House and states that expenditures made by the ex-Minister of Militia, when he was in office, were extravagant expenditures. He instanced one very large item, the expendi+ure on shovels I wonder if they were scrapped? I think that about $50,000 or $60,000 was paid out for shovels. The Minister of Finance admits that that was an extravagant expenditure, and he intimates, if he does not state it as a fact, that other extravagant expenditures were made in that department, and that in order to protect himself and, as far as he could, safeguard the treasury, he found it necessary to write a letter to
the Prime Minister. The Prime Minister, in his letter to the ex-Minister of Militia, states that hie time for several months was taken up with settling quarrels and differences between the ex-minister and other members of the Cabinet. To hand over to this Government on their own demand the enormous sum of $500,000,000, to be expended without our having any further information than we have now, is a rather hard proposal to put before the people's representatives.
The discussion. this afternoon started on the report of Dr. Bruce. I would not assert that the Prime Minister would endeavour to mislead the House or the country, but his statement regarding Dr. Bruce's report was certainly a misleading one. It misled me, and I venture to say that it would mislead the people. The Prime Minister asserted very emphatically that he would not discuss Dr. Bruce's report until it was laid.on the table of the House-indeed, that, until it should be .laid on the table, the report should not be generally discussed. He said further that he had cabled to London for copies of the report and that about forty copies would very shortly be available for distribution. From that one would infer that the report had been published in England but had never come to this country. However, in answer to a question that I put this afternoon, we have been informed by the ex-Minister of Militia that Dr. Bruce's report had been sent to him in September last and has been in the possession of the Government since that time. An order of the House has been passed for the production of this, report, and I cannot understand either why the Department of Militia has not produced it or why the Prime Minister has not seen that it was produced. The subsequent report is also in the department, and I think the Government is very much to blame for misleading the House and the country, even if not intentionally, by giving the impression that that report is not available, whereas it is in their own possession.
I quite understand that it is very much easier to sit outside and criticise what is being done within than to sit inside and improve what is being done. It is not diflicult to criticise,, but it may be difficult to administer the various departments in a time like this. Certain matters, however, can and should he very considerably improved. The House will adjourn, supposedly tomorrow. The Government have established a National Service Commission, ostensibly

in order to ascertain, what can be done further in the way of recruiting; but they do not deign to tell us what definite action they purpose taking in the matter of recruiting. Recruiting is practically at a standstill. On Sunday, January 21, a recruiting campaign was begun in the town of Welland in order to get recruits for the 176th Battalion. The town and the county of Welland and the whole Niagara district have done admirably in the matter of recruiting. This district has made a splendid record for t itself. Diligent .and intelligent work in connection with this recruiting campaign was carried on for a week, with the result that only three recruits were obtained. There are a large number of men in that town and throughout the county who could go to the front. Why do they not go? I will tell the Prime Minister and the Minister of Militia why they do not go. There are in Canada thousands of militiamen who have volunteered for overseas service-they may be found ar Niagara Falls, St. Catharines and other points. These men are officered by men who are drawing their pay simply for the sake of drawing it; who have no intention of going to the front, and who would not be allowed to go to the front even if they went to England. The young men in that district and throughout Canada generally know this, and they say: if men are needed, why do they not send the men that they have? The Colonel of the 176th battalion, who is a Conservative, representing the county of Welland in the local Legislature, made a statement along these lines at a recruiting meeting: The press report says:
The commander of the 176th explained that he had brought 623 from Camp Borden to Niagara Falls and had since taken on 125 men, hut owing to discharges for medical unfitness and desertions the strength of the battalion was only 648.
Or only 25 more than they had. when they came from Camp Borden. One hundred men had deserted or been discharged for unfitness. At the city of St. Catharines they have the 213th Battalion, which, for some unknown reason, is called the American Legion. This battalion has a full complement of officers-colonel, majors and captains-men who will not go to the front and who cannot go even if they want to; and the battalion has only about 213 men. The number may be even less, because I was told on excellent authority that the men were deserting. Then there is the 176th, also with a full complement of officers and 600 men. There you have two battalions and two sets of officers, but scarcely enough

men altogether to make up one battalion. Is that a situation which would, appeal to the young men throughout the locality as being satisfactory? Is it not rather discouraging? If that is the prevailing situation throughout this country, that we have numbers of battalions in different localities one-lialf or less than one-half strength but with a full complement of officers, it being known that these officers will not go to the front and that they are drawing pay, why, in all reason and sensibleness, does not the Government bulk these men and send to the front all men who are fit to go? They want to go, they are appealing to be allowed to go. They do not want to stay here with the training they have had. Why does not the Government send the men to the front where they wish to go and where they can be of some use, and discharge these officers who are drawing pay? Then you would have some encouragement among the young men of this country to join the colours. I should like to know from the Minister of Militia, and I wish he would tell this House, how many colonels and majors and captains there are in London at this hour drawing pay who are not on actual active service, who will not and cannot go to the front. I know some, and a friend of mine who came from London only a few weeks, ago, a very reputable gentleri m, says that these officers who will not go to the front are having a high time, living at the Carlton and the Savoy at the country's expense. I believe they cannot go to the front, in the first place because they are not qualified, and in the next place because there are no positions for them in the capacity of colonel, major or captain. Now I say that condition of affairs is what is destroying recruiting in this country. I know it, because I have spoken to young men about recruiting. But they have done their bit in recruiting. They are not military men, hut they have done nil they cou?^ do to serve the Empire in getting battalions together. as possible.	In the Tegiments to

They have done their duty, and for the most part they have done it well and patriotically.

It is easy to say that Canadian officers in the United Kingdom should either be sent to the front or sent home. That may sound very well, but the matter should be looked into a little more carefully before my hon. friend makes reflections upon as brave a body of Canadian officers wearing the King's uniform as there are in Great Britain to-day. It is not well that any hon. member of this House should generalize with respect to men who have raised battalions in this country, men who have gone to personal expense, who have spent their time, given their services freely, and faced the perils of an Atlantic voyage ito taike their men across; men who desired to get 'to the front but who .are unable to get -there because the positions are filled

That was his answer and that is the answer that appeals to any one's common sense. Supposing that policy had been followed from the beginning, what would have been the result? Take the case that was brought repeatedly to my attention in England; take the case of a colonel, some prominent man who spent months of ihis time in one of the constituencies represented in this House recruiting a regiment. Hie personal weight and influence -had much to- do with the success of recruiting that regiment. I know of eases in which the colonel had everything to do w-ith the recruiting, not because of bis military ability, but because of his personality, his weight and influence in the community. That man recruited his battalion and when

They probably could tell my hon. friend, but it makes no difference how many are there; they have recruited their regiments, gone over there in good faith; they are ready to go to the front when the opportunity does come, and they are waiting for the opportunity to come. What is the reason for the breaking up of battalions when they go over to Great Britain? The reason is the casualties which have taken place at the front and the need for reinforcements. sent forward have had to be broken up and the officers separated from their commands. Instead of there being criticism of these officers there should be the very opposite of criticism. They do not want to be separated from their regiments, and most of them-I do not say all of them, but I have no information to the contrary-desire the first opportunity of going to the front. Is there any thing to

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That sounds very specious. A man who is quite competent to act as a colonel might not be quite as competent to act as a private. He might be of an age at which he might be quite competent to command men and yet not competent to take his place as a private in the trenches. It is unfair to the gallant body of men in London to cast any such reflections upon their patriotism or courage as that which has been cast upon them by the hon. member for Welland.

I did not intend to impeach the courage or cast any reflection on any of the brave officers in London. I did not intend to do any such thing but I say that there are officers-in London drawing pay who cannot go to the front, who will not go to the front, and whom it is the duty of this Government to return to Canada. Are they to be kept over there? If so, for how long? They have been there for months and some of them for a year or more. I have had something to do with recruiting in the section from which I come and I and others in my locality who are not in the Militia force know a good deal about recruiting. We think that we know something about the military situation as well as the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat. This is one of the things that is interfering with recruiting in Canada. There ought to be a remedy and there is one. Are these men to stay there until the end of the war? The Minister of Finance has just told us that he could not send these Canadian

officers to the front as colonels, majors and captains because they have officers in the trenches who are more capable. They have officers in the trenches who enlisted as privates and who have gained their rank for brave deeds in the trenches and they are filling the place of lieutenants, and captains by promoting men from the ranks. So they should, instead of sending over men who have had no experience in the- trenches, and placing them as colonels and captains over men who are just as good as they are, who have enlisted as privates and who have fought the battles of the country from the beginning. Are they to be supplanted by newcomers without trench experience? Certainly not. They should be rewarded by receiving the positions which become vacant when casualties occur in the superior ranks. These are the men who should be promoted. The hon. gentleman speaks very speciously of the officers there. I have not a word to say of the officers over there as men. I am perfectly willing that a colonel should go over with his regiment.
Should he stay there for six months and receive pay for doing nothing at this particular time when we are voting $500,000,000 for this war, and when the Minister of Finance is asking for $100,000,000 of a war loan? Is that a time when men should stay in London under pay, doing nothing, waiting for an opportunity to go to the front, forsooth! when my hon. friend knows as well as I know, and as the Minister of Militia and the ex-Minister of Militia knows, that these men will never go to the front in the capacity of colonel or major in which they went over to England, because those positions will be filled by the men who are promoted and who are fighting the battles in the trenches?

Mr. Chairman, there is poison gas disseminated in connection with this war from other quarters than the trenches in the German line, and there is sniping equally as disastrous to the cause of the war as that of the 'German 'sharpehooters. I am one of those colonels, commanding officers, of whom the hon. gentlemen who act the part of political snipers in Canada speak so contemptuously in this House and through their press. I think it is well that there is one of those commanding officers present from London to answer face to face some of those who have just as much right to be over there as we have had, but who content themselves with discouraging the public men of Canada who do attempt to set an
example to so many others in Canada wRo might be serving their country, but who decline to do so. One feels almost ashamed to discuss service to one's country from the low standpoint of pay; but as a commanding officer who did not put on his uniform because of any pay attached to it, I would like to say that in the office which I carry on at home, and from which a large proportion of the staff have gone to serve our country, from the manager down to the printer's devil, the average pay of the workmen in that office is the pay that a commanding officer in the Canadian Militia receives for commanding a regiment. I hope that is sufficient illustration to convey to the intelligence of some of those hon. gentlemen to whom the pay of a commanding officer looms so large, that possibly there is some other incentive than to receive the same pay as scores of his own staff that impels him to put on the uniform.
I would like to cite my case as an example of what does prompt a member of Parliament to offer his services at the front. At a certain stage in recruiting in Canada, the then Minister of Militia called for
100,000	additional troops. We have about 100 infantry battalions in Canada, so that meant an overseas battalion, in addition to those already raised, from each of the infantry battaljons in this country. As I had the honour at that time of commanding an infantry regiment in Canada, I felt that it was an appeal to me to raise an overseas battalion, and I promptly volunteered to do it and I did do it.
As the Minister of Finance has said, the personal influence of a commanding officer had a great deal to do at that time in securing recruits. I feel quite sure that the fact that I had the honourable position of a member of the House of Commons gave me a great leverage in going about through my district and asking the young men of Westminster district-not to go to the front, but to come to the front with me. I may say to the hon. gentleman who says that the commanding officers might go as privates that I will forestall his objection by telling him that when I was of the age at which men do go as privates, I went to the front as a private in the service of my country. I am not of that age now and I could not go as a private nor as a lieutenant. If I volunteered I would not be accepted. But I did raise a very fine battalion in my district because of my personal appeals, and, if I do say it, because of what little prestige I have in that district.
