'Under ordinary circu: ^stances I and my battalion might very w jll have gone to the front as a unit. It was our desire. Many a political enemy at home-because we have a few snipers there, although in the West they do not flourish-has caused it to be asked of me on the platform or elsewhere: "Are you going to the front yourself"?-the imputation being that I was doing a grandstand play. I answered them honestly and truthfully that it was my desire and my intention to go to the front. My battalion arrived in England with thirteen others in a convoy, a total of 14,000 troops, immediately after the terrible experience on the Somme. The Canadian Headquarters in London were confronted then with a demand for the immediate services of about 19,000 men to replace the casualties which had just occurred, and it was our fortune when we arrived in England, to be selected as some of those reinforcements which were immediately sent. I think all the battalions in that convoy except two were drafted for that purpose. My battalion sent 400 men to the trenches within two weeks of our arrival in England, 100 a week later, and since then they have been going continuously. Now then, which is the more glorious, which is the more to be commended in a commanding officer, that, being met with a demand there to send men into -the fighting line and having recruited men for the fighting line, he should say: "I have brought these men to fight and they are at your service"; or that he should come to his political headquarters, if he has any political standing, and -say: "Do not send these men to fight, but leave them with me for my honour and glory so that I may go forward as a commanding officer"? What would the hon. gentlemen have isaid 'if it bad. tunned out that I was asked to send 500 men immediately to the trenches and I said: "Do not do that; what position do you put me in; if you send those, I cannot go?" And why could I not go? Because the regiment most calling for men at that time was one from my very own district, the 47th Westminster Battalion straight from the Somme, 400 shy, including in the ranks of officers twelve out of my own home regiment, including hundreds of men the every day aisisociates of those whom I had brought over. What more natural than that my 400 should go to their own neighbours from Westminster, to their own officers of their old regiment? And why could not the Colonel go? Because -greatly to the disappointment, seemingly, of these gentlemen opposite-Colonel Wins-
by, of the 47th, had not been shot; Major Coote second in command, of the 47th, and Major in my regiment at home, had not been shot. They remained in command. Therefore, Colonel Taylor and Major Cunningham of the recently-arrived regiment were not able to go to the front. What would the hon. gentleman have? Am I to be condemned by him and those like him because I took a battalion to England? Am I to be condemned because, having sent my men into the firing line, I come back and take up my duties as a member of this House?
I will show to some of these gentlemen what their criticism of unemployed officers means in some cases. An instance arose in England in June of 1915. A number of senior officers became unpleasantly conscious of their great numbers in England. There were eighty majors, for instance, who said: "Wc'dislike remaining here; we came over to go to the front; let us go forward as supernumerary lieutenants". And they went as supernumerary lieutenants. Now, the supernumerary lieutenant has almost less than no duties. He is the understudy of the lieutenant in charge of a platoon. He is not quite so useful as a sergeant in charge of any section, because the sergeant has been trained with the section from the beginning and is more accustomed to it than the supernumerary lieutenant can be. Not afraid of German bullets, and perhaps too conscious of the criticism such as is offered in this House to-night, these majors said: "Let us go over the parapet with the men". They went. Only twenty came back. Are we to cheer in this House because in that one stroke we wiped out sixty superfluous majors?
The hon. gentleman asks why these men are not sent home at once. The answer is so plain that I wonder that anyone should ask the question with a desire of obtaining knowledge. If asked with the idea that, being unanswered, it will make a point to the discredit of the soldiers of Canada, the question seems more intelligible. I would like to hear in upon the consciousness of some of these hon. gentlemen the fact that a senior military officer is not made in five minutes. And, as it takes a long time to make him, so it should take a correspondingly long time to arrive at the conclusion that he should be discarded and sent home. As the training proceeds in Canada, there are technical courses of all kinds to qualify the officers for the duties they are to exercise at the front. When we are asked

to send an officer to a school at Quebec, to a school at Ottawa, or Winnipeg, or Victoria, as I was asked from time to time to send mine, the accompanying note nearly always is: Send a senior officer, if possible. And properly so; because a senior officer should be qualified to lead in every branch of instruction. In the case of my battalion, nearly every senior officer bad 'been the subject of a special course of training at some of these schools, to the exclusion of the junior officers, because the number was limited.
They attended several schools in some cases.

Some of these officers had attended several schools, as the former Minister of Militia reminds me. Now, what would have been said of this Government if the moment these highly trained officers arrived in London they were told: " Since you cannot go forward with your battalion, you had better go straight home?" Then 'we should have had a political scandal. -
As to unemployment in London, as to the presence of officers in hotels in London, I wonder where these hon. gentlemen get their information. During the two months I spent in the Old Country, I was in London, I suppose, five or six times. On every occasion when I was there I had been sent for by an officer of higher command in London for some specific business. My visits there, I suppose, were generally for two days at a time-'business starting to-day and finishing to-morrow. As these hon. gentlemen see it, I was one of the officers, " crowding the hotels in London." I saw no officers there during my time who were not properly there. The majority of them were on leave from the front, the few weeks' leave that the officer gets after a great many months of service. The minority were of my class, officers who had come to England with the bona fide intention of going to the front, and who bad not achieved their ambition. I do not think a large percentage of these officers were in what we would call an idle class, or that by their presence or their actions they constituted a reflection upon the Canadian military service. It seemed to me they were an exceptionally fine body of men. We are 'asked why they spent months there instead of coming home. I had an illustration. I will not mention names, because to do so would be like advertising that the officer to whom I refer had spent so many months idle. I found in a camp to which I went in England one of the very finest officers in British Columbia, a man,
perhaps, fifteen or twenty years my junior, trained in every respect, who had brought over a battalion equal in merit to any battalion that had left our province, but a battalion that, like my own, was broken up on arrival there. That man had come across with no other idea than that of serving at the front. He had closed all hi's affairs in Canada. He was not even a member of Parliament, and could not have a member of Parliament's excuse-these hon. gentlemen seem to think it is 'an excuse-d,o come back to Canada. He waited for employment- He got employment the day I left England, that is, nine months after arrival there. He got the remnant of his own battalion, the remnant of my battalion, and the remnant of the 158th Battalion of Vancouver, to be under hi's command as the 1st British Columbia Training Battalion. And a fine training officer he is. Why should we criticise that officer for .having -been compelled to wait that time? These hon. gentlemen speak, in connection with this, as in connection with all other military subjects we have heard discussed in the House, as if they were the discoverers of something which, if they were the Government, would be done, but which is not done by this seemingly neglectful Administration.
We are told that the administration in London should grapple with the question of unemployment. These gentlemen opposite must know-because they have read it in their own press, paragraph	after paragraph-that the subject is being grappled with. They know that about two months ago a board was appointed to examine in detail into the standing of every officer not in serious employment in England; that this board visited every Canadian camp in England, questioned all the officers, as well as men of other ranks, as to their capacity and as to whether they could profitably take up military service other than what they had gone to England to do. The men were then divided into three categories: those who could advantageously be sent to the front and be replaced in England by others returning from the front; those who could do nothing at the front or in England, but might with advantage be given permission to return to Canada-because you cannot return without permission-and those who could profitably continue to be employed in London or in other parts of England. The question was dealt with in the most serious manner at that time by a board of very competent officers, several of whom

had seen service at the front, some of whom had served with distinction there and, having come back to London, found themselves temporarily unemployed. If an abuse had crept in, they were instructed to see that that abuse was discontinued, and they were inspired with a desire that it should be discontinued. No doubt as a result of the report of that board, officers have returned, opportunity has been found to send officers to France, and every opportunity has been taken to substitute the services of returned soldiers for services that had been performed in the Old Country by Canadians who had not been to the front. When the officers are moved on under these circumstances, I do not think they should be pilloried as having been driven to do something that they were unwilling to do. I prefer to take the view that the officers who go there, do so in good faith, ready to lay themselves on the altar of their country and to make whatever sacrifices they may be called upon to make. Do these hon. gentlemen opposite realize for a moment that soldiering is not eight hours' work a day during .six days of the week? Do they realize that there are a great many soldiers in England and in France who are not in the firing line; that there are a great many private soldiers who are unemployed in quite as wide a sense as these officers are unemployed, and that it is absolutely true that these men are serving their country efficiently and nobly? We have millions of soldiers in reserve in England and France who are not working every day, or six days a week, just the same as we have some idle officers. These soldiers are kept for the great drive which we all anticipate, and which only can change the condition from that of apparent stalemate now prevailing. Are they to be pilloried as men who are eating the bread of idleness in England? Is it .fair to our soldiers who remain in Canada, hawing been trained here, that they should be pilloried, as is the custom to-day, not only occasionally in the House, but also in the party press? Are they not just as useful to us in reserve in Canada, waiting to go to England and. France when they 'are sent for, as they would be if we got them out of our sight by sending them to England or to France? Are we improving the cause of the war by having nothing but criticism-small-souled, mean-spirited criticism, if I may use the expression-of those who try to serve the Empire, but who are not permitted to dlo so to the extent that 
they desire? It seems to me, as an officer who has, had much experience in recruiting, that more harm has been done to the cause of recruiting in Canada by the state-(inemts made this .session from the other side of the House .and widely diesemimaited as they have been, for political purposes iby the party press-the fountainheads of the poisoned political gas in this country- than by any possible combination of errors on the part of the Government.

I have (been very much
interested in the remarks of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Taylor). I do not wish to criticise them, except to say that his entire speech was absolutely spoiled by the bitter partisanship of hds last few words.
Oh, oh.
Shame.
One would think, to hear him speak of poisoned gas, that we on this side had no interest in the war. *
It seems to fit well.

My hon. friend, who is always interrupting, may say what he likes, but this is too serious a matter to be allowed to pass. If we on this side, who have made as many sacrifices as my hon. friend has in this war-some of us have devoted as much time as he has to matters affecting the war -are not to he allowed to criticise simply because he does not like it, then this is not a free country, and the liberties that we pretend to be fighting for he purposes taking away from us.
I do not purpose taking away any liberties. You have just told us what you pretend to be fighting for in the House, and I agree with you.
What fare you fighting for?

He is not fighting for anything. I Teally do not understand what my hon. friend means. I wish to point out that any criticism that we have made has not been such as was indicated by my hon. friend. He has said that the criticism has been made solely for party purposes. I want to tell him that there are men on this side of the House who have an interest in seeing that our share in the war is conducted in the best possible manner with regard not only to the safety of the Empire, but also to the safety of the men iat the front. It is our purpose to criticise in order to bring about that result, and if my hon. friend considers that to be against the best

interest of the Allies, then he has not the judgment that I think he ought to have.
What I said was that untrue statements disseminated from the House had injured the cause of recruiting.
My hon. friend said that the criticism indulged in during this session had injured recruiting.
So it has.
My hon. friend thinks it has. He has been here all the time, and he does not know about the outside.
Neither do you.

I have delivered several recruiting speeches since the session opened. I say that just such speeches as my hon. friend (Mr. Taylor) has made have done injury to the cause of recruiting. We want to work in harmony with the Government in everything that will conduce to the best interests of Canada and the Empire, and I leave it to the serious judgment of the men on the Government side who do things as to whether or not that is the case. F.ut if we .are to be scolded because we criticise and make suggestions, then I say, Sir, that what we pretend to be. fighting for is a myth. The full liberty of the member to discuss is given to' us by the constitution of this country, and the more acute the situation is the more it is right, and the more it is our duty, to criticise, if that criticism will conduce to the best interests of the cause we all have at heart. Now this attempt to create discord, I do not think is the proper thing. I was deeply interested in the remarks of my hon friend (Mr. Taylor). He is a man who can speak with some knowledge of the conditions and of the situation in which he found himself. I took more than ordinary interest in what he said, and I might tell him that I was more than interested; I felt that he had spoken from his heart as to the conditions. But, Sir, when he turns on us and insists that we are doing something injurious to the cause of the Empire, and gives us a lecture. intimating that we have not the cause of the Empire at heart, I want to tell him that he is altogether wrong, and that we on this side of the House have as much right to free speech, and are as much interested in the war, as hon gentlemen opposite. And when the history of this country comes to'be written, it will be found that the criticism made by members on this side of the House has helped and not hindered the cause of the Empire.

I listened with a great deal of interest to the remarks made by the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Taylor) and I would like to add one or two words. I did not understand nor do I think the members of this House understood that the member for New Westminster was charging against the Liberal members of this House or the Liberal party as a whole that they should not make any criticism whatever. He stated that in this House during this session there had been criticisms offered on this Government which were 'founded on untrue statement, and that those untrue statements, offered in the form of criticisms, were hurtful to recruiting. And in making that statement he said what every man in this House knows to be absolutely true. I want to ask my hon. friend if he thinks the statement made the other day by the member for Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff) that because of the retempering of the bolts of the Ross rifle hundreds of lives had been sacrificed at the front was in the interest of recruiting. It was pointed out to him that that retempering took place last year, and not one of those rifles was in the hands of those men. But that makes no difference to that gentleman; his statement has gone upon Hansard, it has been caught up by certain of the party press, and sent out to the country. Was he man enough then to get up on the floor and retract his statements and say he had made a mistake? We had another instance in the case of the hon. member for Lamb-ton (Mr. Pardee), who pours out a tale of woe about a returned soldier in Windsor who came back to Canada, was allowed to pass through the country without any overcoat, who had frozen his hands and feet and all that sort of thing; and he wound up by saying that he had no doubt there were hundreds of cases just like this throughout the country. That goes through the country, it is picked up by the press and circulated. The proof in that case lies in the fact that members belonging to the Soldiers' Relief Committee in Windsor sent to the hon. member for North Essex (Mr. Wilcox) a telegram, which was read here to-night at six o'clock, to the effect that the statement of the hon. member for Lambton, as published in the press, was absolutely false. When challenged with that to-night at six o'clock by the hon. member for North Essex, what did the hon. member for Lambton say? He said: I merely read what was in the press, what was stated in the newspaper, that is all that I did. That is

not all that he did, for he followed up that statement, without trying to ascertain whether it was authentic, by his statement that he did not doubt there were hundreds of cases like that. This is the kind of statements made by the hon. gentlemen opposite to which the hon. member for New Westminster referred when he said, and truly said, that statements are made on the floor of the House by hon. gentlemen opposite that are a hindrance to recruiting. Does the member for Renfrew (Mr. Graham) think that his presence on the platform at a political meeting in the city of Toronto, when a man by the name of Hartley Dewart went into details and disregarded facts in regard to the exportation of nickel, and was supported and endorsed by the presence of the hon. gentleman on the platform-does he think that attitude was a proper one and in the interest of recruiting? I for one do not think it was.
Mr. Speaker, this war has demonstrated this fact, that we have, over at the front, Canadians who never were known in the public life of this country before, who wert considered small men if you like, hardly recognizable, but who have proved themselves to be big men in every sense of the word. It has also been demonstrated on the floor of this Parliament that we have men who have been in the public eye as representative men, holding seats in this Parliament, who have shown by their attitude and their words that they are small men-small men and very small. Talk about their conscience being affected by the Ross rifle and that sort of thing! The stain is not in the conscience of hon. gentlemen opposite; for I say to them: if you will look down to your finger tips you will find that the stain is produced by your attempt, for political purposes, to turn the bloody key in the door of office and to open the portals to yourselves.

After this scolding which we have received from our friend, with the true (Germanic spirit which prevents him from permitting any man in this free country to say anything in this Parliament or out of it, or to venture in any way to disagree with him, I wish to read some extracts from a letter which I have received from another Colonel; not my hon. friend from New Westminster (Mr. Taylor), but a colonel who left this country for the war in 1914 and has not come home yet. I read this just for the purpose of telling my hon. friend who has just sat down that there are some people in this country who do not

agree with him, and who do not agree with our colonel friend from New Westminster. The letter is of such a character that if I read it in full detail my hon. friend who has just sat down would at once proceed to scold me and to scold the colonel, because he would say the publication of such statements would prevent recruiting in this country. I shall read one or two extracts and leave it to this House, once we have got back to our normal frame of mind and after the lecture which the hon. member for New Westminster has given us, as to whether or not there is justification for hon. gentlemen on this side saying something about the conduct of the war. This letter came to me unsolicited; I had no communication with this gentleman in any way whatever. It came to me in the month of December, and among the expressions which he makes use of is the following:
If the people of Canada knew what goes on here in the waste of public money, the creation of jobs for disgruntled politicians and wire pullers, it would make very interesting reading for the Canadian people.
What is his name?
I will give to the Minister of Militia, if he desires, the name of this colonel.

As one having the interest of the soldiers at heart, I respectfully submit that the hon. member should not give out the name of the officer. I have never heard of this case, but I do not like to see the name of an officer brought in.
If it is bad form for this colonel over in England, who is not a political colonel, to write certain remarks of this kind, what is the form of the Colonei from New Westminster?
I do not think my hon. friend should give the officer away.
The colonel from New Westminster is not anonymous or ashamed of what he said.

This gentleman is not anonymous. If it comes to a question of pluck and achievement, the gentlemen of whom I am speaking will compare with the hon. member for New Westminster. He did not spend two months in England; he went over in 1914, and has not come home yet. He goes on:
If the facts that exist here were known in Canada-but our mouths are closed as long as we wear uniforms.

Where is that from, is
it from France?

No, it is written
from a camp in England. If my hon. friend wants to suggest any question about this letter, I pledge my word as a member of this House that I will give the name of the writer to the Minister of Militia. '
What is he doing in England?

He is at work in
England at the present time. He goes on further:
The impression with many officers is that the young life's blood of Canada is exploited to glorify the Tory party, and I must admit that it seems to be true.
Oh, oh.

What further does the- gentleman say:
I do not know whether the censor will pass this or not. If he does not I hope he will pass it on to the Government for I am going to sign my name to it and dare any one to contradict anything written here.
I have stated what I am prepared to do in regard to the matter. I desire to say that if, as has been suggested by the ex-Minister of Militia (Sir Sam Hughes) that this colonel, who went over in August, 1914, and has not yet seen his home or family, is not permitted to express his opinion in regard to the conditions over there without being denounced by hon. gentlement opposite, my hon. friend from Westminster (Mr. Taylor) has no right to lecture the men who sit on this side of the House when there are in France the graves of three boys, sons of members, and when there are some twenty-five to thirty members on this side of the House whose boys are over there. We need no lectures from hon. gentlemen opposite on this question.
But what your friend says is not true.
I will put the word of the man who wrote this statement against the word of my hon. friend.
It is not true.
Who is he?
I have told my hon. friend from Annapolis what I will do with respect to the name. I merely rose for the purpose of showing that there are colonels on the other side who have something to say.
I said that the statement is absolutely untrue.

Here is the letter
with the signature to it, and I am prepared to show it to the Prime Minister or to the Minister of Militia at any moment. These statements are made by a man who left here two and a half years ago, and there is no justification whatever for the suggestion that hon. members on this side of the House should not indulge in reasonable criticism. What criticism has ever been made in this House so keen as that made by the ex-Minister of Militia (Sir Sam Hughes), who declared that if the conditions as he found them to exist at one time in England were permitted to continue under the administration of a new Minister of Militia, the forces would be reduced to a chaotic condition. Has there been anything more emphatic than that statement? Could any stronger criticism be made?

What I said had
reference to the statement that political action had been taken on the other side during the last nine months or during whatever time that officer has been over there. What I meant to say was that under my administration, I challenge the face of clay to point to a single instance of political preferment.
I shall be very glad to show this letter to my hon. friend. He knows this colonel.

If I was Minister
of Militia I would refuse to look at a letter of that kind from an officer, because it immediately brings him under the law. That was my reason for suggesting that he should not divulge the name to the Prime Minister except in confidence.

An officer who is a
member of Parliament has a double advantage, and certain exemptions.

An officer is always permitted to' criticise favourably, but he is not permitted to criticise adversely.
Some' hon. MEMBERS: Oh, oh.
That is the law of the country.

This gentleman
writes this letter expecting that it might not pass the censor. He makes the stater ment which I have read.
I made the suggestion for the protection of the officer.
I have quoted from this letter for the purpose of showing that there are men on the other side of the Atlantic to-day who have gone from Canada, and who have certain opinions about

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
Who says that the
hon. gentleman has no such right?
We have had an intimation fro-m my hon. friend from Westminster.

No, no.
- Mr. TAYLOR:	I rise -to a -question of
privilege. I a-mi being misquoted by the hon. member. My reference was solely to untrue and unfair criticism -from the other side of the House.
These are not the words you used, as you will see in Hansard.

My hon. friend made a general statement in regard to criticism from this side of the House, and I appeal to the judgment of this committee whether in the discussions that have taken- place iwe have not been entirely within our rights in asking for information, in discussing the [DOT]merits of the Ross rifle, or in discussing the question of the reports of Dr. Bruce and Dr. Baptie.
Dr. Bruce is in Canada to-night.

I am aware of that. 1 submit to this committee and to the House that we have a perfect right to criticise, and that we cannot be asked to abrogate our constitutional functions as representatives of the people in discussing these matters. We have had tremendous expenditures during the -past two years. We have had the great question of recruiting, the question as to whether or not recruiting

has been properly carried on, and the question as to whether or not the aim of the Prime Minister as to raising 500,000 men c$m be realized. What sense is there in declaring that in regard to matters like these silence should reign, and that no man shall criticise or make suggestion. It is for the maintenance forever of that right in this country that we are fighting against a system which would prevent that criticism, the system which prevails in Germany, a militarism that wants to dominate the world. Our criticism has been legitimate and proper, and it has been within our rights.	'

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Let me note a specific instance. What -does my hon. friend think of the statement made by the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff) to the effect that the Prime Minister had stated before the Ontario Recruiting League that it was his desire that there should be no more recruiting in Canada? What is his opinion as to that statement? Does he consider it fair criticism?
My hon. friend wants me to discuss a question of difference of opinion between the hon. member for As-siniboi-a and the Prime Minister.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: A difference of opinion! Does the hon. gentleman agree with the hon. member for Assiniboia?
Probably the end of that matter has not been heard of. I am not here to discuss details. That is a personal matter between the hon. member for Assiniboia and the Prime Minister.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Not at all. The hon. member for Assiniboia does -not claim to have been present at the meeting. The Prime Minister was there, and he specifically and emphatically denies the statement; but there has been no retraction by the hon. member for Assiniboia, and- no one has come to his rescue.
Let me -suggest to the Solicitor General that possibly we have not' heard the end of the matter.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Give us the end of it now.

My hon. friend from Assin-ifooi-a is no-t here. Were he here he would be perfectly able to take care of himself. I do not think the hon. member for F-rontenac (Mr. Edwards) was fair to the Liberal party with regard to his address

yesterday. Everyone who knows that the hon. member for West Lambton (Mr. Pardee) knows that he is not a gentleman who assails this House with extreme utterances at any time, but on the 'altogether too ra/re occasions upon which he has addressed the House he has not done so offensively or in such a way as to entitle him to he regarded as in any way extreme. The right hon. the Prime Minister yesterday complimented my hon. friend from West Lambton on the manner in which he bad 'brought the attention of the House and the country to the duty which we are called upon to perform in reference to our returned soldiers. That speech was not regarded by the right hon. Prime Minister as having been the result of any idea of imputing blame to the Government at all. Every hon. gentleman who heard 'the hon. member for West Lambton knows that his 'speech was not of a controversial character and was not intended to impute blame to the Government. He asked for the -best possible good and with the best of intentions that .both sides of this House should join in the appointment of a committee to take into their most careful and serious consideration this great problem in the interim between now and the resumption of the session. It 'is only fair to my hon. friend who is not here that I should make this statement in reference to him.
In regard to the whole question of this debate, I regret that at this stage there should be any manifestation of feeling in reference to it. The ex-Minister of Militia refers to the fact that Dr. Bruce is in Canada. I understand that Dr. Bruce has arrived in Canada and in order that we may bring the discussion of this question back to where we started this afternoon I would like to ask the Prime Minister, as I am informed Dr. Bruce is preparing to make some statement to the Canadian people with regard to the question of the examination which he ha's made into medical conditions on the other side, whether he will not endeavour to give us to-morrow, before the House adjourns, the reports made by Dr. Bruce and Dr. Baptie, if they are in his possession. I understand from the statement of the ex-Minister of Militia that the report of Dr. Bruce is in the department.
Let us have it on the table of 11 p.m the House to-morrow so that in the consideration of this matter, if there is to be any statement made by Dr. Bruce the House and the country will be seized of the facts in regard to the whole question after seeing the reports of Dr. Bruce and Dr. Baptie.

I am not going to
take any part in any of the pros and cons.
I have been in the House for twenty-seven sessions and I have to express my regret at the quarrelings and contentions, backwards and forwards, over a great question of this kind. It is quite unseemly. But, I always appreciate criticism and I think I have had as much nasty criticism as any gentleman present. Last spring the Globe came out with an editorial attacking the department for having 200 or 300 officers lying around England idle. A short time after the troops first went over we had no 'Staff, and no officers attached to the staff. They were taken from the various regiments as they passed over. These officers, although acting as staff officers, had to appear on the roll cf the regiments as colonels, majors and captains. They were taken from the regiments and they were not on the headquarters or the various divisional or brigade staffs. These officers, could not draw their pay and allowances for staff work because they were only attached to regiments. The pay master General across the water mentioned that there were 200 or 230 odd officers attached to regiments who were not drawing pay and allowances and some clever editor, seeing it, thought there were 200 or more officers in England unattached. Then, writers up and down the country, of course to help the cause and not at all with the intention of injuring the Tory party or the Minister of Militia, but to help the cause and to make the boys over there feel more at home and the friends and mothers of the boys more comfortable here came out with column after column attacking the Department of Militia and Defence for having these 200 odd officers in England for whom there was nothing to do. But every officer was act- ' ively employed. Shortly 'after this occurred there came the Zillebeke affair in June. I had an application, through our staff, from the War Office for upwards of 200 officers and I had an application when I was in England to send over 400 officers to fill the places of the boys who had gone.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Six hundred altogether?

Nearly 600 altogether to go and fill the gaps. We did not have the officers there. I gave instructions that well-educated, intelligent, capable boys, sergeants, corporals and privates in the ranks should be promoted, and hundreds of these boys were promoted. I did not take the criticism seriously. I rather enjoyed it. I think I have told the story told by

Barnum the first time I saw him when I was a boy. He said: I spend $75,000 a year to have the show condemned, and I spend $750,000 to have the show advertised. I get ten times as much value out of the $75,000 that I spend to have the show condemned as I do out of the $750,000 that I spend to have the show advertised. Everybody copies the condemnation and nobody believes it, but the advertisement is all the greater. I have learned to proceed upon that line. There has been a great deal of criticism, but it does not affect me.
Now, I want to say a word about getting the battalions across the sea. I am going to make this statement that in all the recruiting that has ever been carried on in civilized warfare, or any other kind of warfare, none has equalled that which has been carried on in Canada. We sent the officers who recruited these battalions over with them. There was some criticism, but I paid m>
attention to it. I felt that people, such for instance as my friend Taylor here, who had raised regiments, were entitled to take their regiments across, and serve a few weeks at all events with their regiments. Then we gave them what we called a Cook's tour to the front, where they would get a little experience and a great deal of information, so that they might be able to come back home and give Canada the benefit of the experience and information which they had acquired. I took that view, and it has been proved to be the practical and proper view of the matter, and it has been carried out. There is no doubt that there are a number of these fellows who are good fellows, the very best in the world, whose whole hearts are in the cause, like my friend Taylor here, who went to work and did their best, although they knew that their chances of getting to the front were more or less hazy. But they wanted to go. One member of this House, Col. Arthurs-I read the most touching letter I have seen for many a day-is in the trenches. He had reduced his rank and gone over in spite of his son's remonstrance from the trenches ordering his dad to get out. These officers went over in command. They knew that the chances were that a great majority of their battalions would have to be broken up for draft purposes. But, there is nothing wrong in having these officers overseas. It was due to their efforts that many of these regiments were recruited. Colonel Taylor, for instance, was the most powerful recruiting agent one could have in his district. I think these men were entitled to a trip over and a little visit

there; it does not cost a great deal, and they are doing something useful. When they return to their homes, they will have acquired further experience, and they will be able to do even better work in the way of recruiting in Canada. Before I left England I gave directions for the organization of a committee. I demanded a report of every officer employed in England at that time. The report was not completed when I came away, and the instructions were to classify the officers, as my hon. friend has stated, into three classes and then to select those who were suitable for a command, and if possible, to give them an opportunity.
I want to say another word about the Fifth Division and the boys at the front. I am satisfied-and I do not want to go further than to express my own views- that we can have a Fifth Division and, if necessary, a Sixth and a Seventh and an Eighth Division at the front, from the men whom we now have across the water. That proposition I put in black and white to Sir Douglas Haig, Sir William Kobertson and Mr. Lloyd George, now Prime Minister. My purpose was to have as many as possible of those men trained, and we have heard here to-night how men were taken over to France the second week they were in England, with no more experience than that, and put right into the trenches. I can tell of men who, within a week after their arrival in England, were sent over to France, and who the first morning after they arrived in France, were wounded and some of them killed, so that there is nothing in the story about the necessity of Canadian soldiers being kept in England for training purposes. They learn more in a week in the trenches than they do in a month in England or in Canada. My proposition was to put as many divisions at the front as we possibly could, to have a certain frontage and to take care of that and no more. Our casualties would be no greater if we had six divisions than if we had four divisions, because we would have only a certain length of front, and the men I am satisfied would be more healthy in France than they are in England. In that way we would have six divisions trained ready for action in the great drive which is coming on at an early date, whereas now we shall have only four divisions trained for it. There should be two Canadian Army Corps at the front, one which I would like to see under the command of General Turner and the other under the command of General Currie. I should imagine that

General Turner is sick of his job in London and that he would be glad to get back to the music of the guns. If General Byng has to be disposed of, he should be made an officer commanding an army because the Canadian boys like him. I do not wish to bring up anything controversial; but the whole matter is very easy: We have plenty of men across ithe water, and the few 'that 'are in England can very well get on without General Turner.

speakeroldname: Mr. W. F. CARROLL (South Cape Breton) :
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I do not arise for
the purpose of criticising the Militia Department of this country. I could, of course, under my privilege as a member of the House of Commons criticise the department, ibut I am not entitled to criticise it outside, and I am not going to say anything in this House which I am not permitted to say on the hustings of this country.

If my hon. friend
will permit me, he is all wrong. If he will read the address I gave to this House in the year 1901 in the Hutton matter, he will see the law laid down there on the subject. He can from his seat here to-night, or on the street to-morrow, if the House is in session, tell the Prime Minister, or the Minister of Militia, or the ex-Minister of Militia exactly what he thinks of them, positively or negatively, and no man can lay a finger on him under the law. Admiral Napier left the fleet in front of Kronstadt and came back to the House of Commons and pounded the life out of the Admiralty.

What the ex-minister
has stated was what I was trying to point out. Perhaps I did not make myself quite clear, that I was allowed as a member of this House to criticise the military authori-' ties and, indeed, any person, even the King; but when the House is not in session, I am not allowed to do it outside, and I do not purpose saying anything in this House or outside while the House is in session that I am not permitted to say outside while the House is not in session. i I am sorry I was not in the House yesterday when the matter of looking after returned soldiers was under discussion. Last evening I received from a personal friend of mine in the city of Sydney, who (by the way is a very strong party man and who happens to be a Conservative, a letter regarding the matter of looking after our returned soldiers and also giving some strictures regarding the appointment of censors around the Marconi stations. He
takes' the ground that a great many of our men, who should be at the front to-day or who should 'be training for service at the front, were given positions as decoders or censors at those stations at the beginning of the war, and that they should be relieved to-day and their positions given to returned soldiers. We have in the island of Cape Breton a considerable number of returned soldiers who would make excellent decoders and censors. It strikes me that in the matter of appointing decoders and censors, the Government undertook to appoint men who in some cases had private incomes, who ini many other cases had large wages and who are receiving the same large wages to-day. The names that I have in my hand are all those of censors; my friend does not mention the decoders at all. I wish it to be understood that I am saying nothing against any of these men or their capacities as censors; I have no doubt that the censors are good censors and that the decoders are good decoders. Mr. D. S. Hooper of Louisburg is assistant censor and at the present time is receiving $5 per day. He is Superintendent of Government Telegraph at a salary of $600 per year with horse-hire, and he is also local manager of the Maritime Telegraph and Telephone Company at a salary of $500 per year.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: When was he appointed?

He was appointed at least two years ago. I know a gentleman in the town of Glace Bay, a man who went over with either the Pioneers or the Tun-nellers, Mr. Dan McDougall-and he is not a political friend of mine-
Is that old Dan?
Yes, old Dan McDougall. He was returned some time ago as being medically unfit. He is a man of considerable education.
He was concerned in the strike?
He was the leader of the United Mine Workers' strike?
He is a very good fellow.

A good man. I am mentioning his name because I know him personally. He is a man of education, if not a man of means. I think in justice to Mr. McDougall it would be well for whoever

has charge of the Censorship Branch that this matter should be looked into. When Mr. MeDougall came back from the front, medically unfit for service, he could not get anything to do, and he had to go into the mines to work, although that is rather strenuous work for a person who is medically unfit for military service.
Then there is another man, Mr. W. T. Hayden, who is assistant censor at $4 per day. He is also private secretary to Mr. J. C. Douglas who has the patronage of Cape Breton county so far as military matters are concerned and who is a member of the legislature.
Is Mr. Douglas a Tory?

Yes. Then there is Mr. Charles Macdonald who my informant states is decoding clerk at a salary of $3.25 per day, but I think as a matter of fact the salary for decoding clerks is $2.50. Mr. Macdonald is law clerk with Mr. J. C. Douglas. Then there is Mr. E. L. Gilpin of North Sydney who is censor at the cable office at a salary of $7 per day. He is also property agent of the Dominion Iron and Steel Company at a salary of $3,000 per year, and secretary of the Steel Workers' Benefit Fund at a salary of $1,200 per year I think we have some returned officers, who, having been wounded at the front, have been sent back as medically unfit, who would be well suited for a position of that kind. Not that Mr. Gilpin is not able to fill the position, but because he seems to be a man moderately well off, judging from the salary he gets. Another gentleman to whom I would refer is Mr. E. O. Burke, a very fine, estimable gentleman. He is assistant censor in the cable office at five dollars a day. He is also employed with the Dominion Iron and Steel Company at a salary of $1,800 a year. Then we come to Mr. B. Archibald, of North Sydney, who is assistant censor at the cable office at five dollars a day. He is also stipendiary magistrate of the town of North Sydney and carries on a legal business in that town. The gentleman who sends me the information says that he is a man of independent means. If he said he was wealthy I think he would be nearer the mark. Though Mr. Archibald is one of the first gentlemen in our country, yet if he weTe relieved of that job and some returned soldier who had the capacity to do this work were given the position I think it would be an advantage.

There are a few grievances under which I think the soldiers at the front are 'suffering at this time, and I intend to ask the Minister of Militia the privilege of writing to him a letter to tell him in my own humble way of the things that I think should be remedied. It is not my intention to criticise, as I have said. In any case, the Government might not be the 'subject of criticism, as it migbt be that officers in England are responsible for the grievances. If the Minister of Militia will give me the privilege, I will bring these matters to his attention in a letter; or, if he would prefer it, I will see him in his office, and in an interview discuss them with him.
That is all I have to say. I think that the Government should take into consideration this matter of the censorship, not only in the places to which I have referred, but generally, because I think the same conditions hold elsewhere. Where men are able to earn a living otherwise, yet are given large salaries as most of these men are, they should be relieved of these positions and the positions given to returned soldiers, who are capable of filling them.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada

speechtext: There is nothing very technical about this business. The men who are now in office went in knowing nothing about the censorship, and depending simply upon their instructions.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
I did not say there was anything technical about it, but that it takes a degree of intelligence above the ordinary, as well as education and maturity of judgment more than can be secured for very small remuneration. But, while the standard of service must be maintained, yet, subject to that, the returned soldier must get the preference. I shall be glad to review what the hon. gentleman has said, and to make a specific investigation in every case.-

One of the effects of the war has been to cause people to open their hearts and sympathies not only to those engaged in the war, but to all other needy people. Never in the history of Canada have the poor been so well looked after as they have been since the war began; the greater the burden imposed upon the people, the greater the burden they seem able and willing to bear. We are taking a new outlook: viewing things from a different angle. I want to bring to the attention of the Minister of Finance a case which, I think, deserves his consideration. Probably no legal right is involved, but when we are gladly preparing to look after those who are injured in the cause of Canada and the Empire, I think we may, without creating a precedent and without doing anything but honour to ourselves, consider a case of this kind. I refer to the case of Colin C. McNab, now a resident of Braeside, who was engaged by the Canadian Pacific Railway as a telegraph operator during the Northwest Rebellion. According to the information given to me by him, he was placed by the company in charge of officers of the militia. His pay came indirectly from the Government. He worked day and night for months during many long weary hours in the Northwest, and as a result of disease contracted fin that employment he lost his eyesight and has since been blind. He has been groping his way through life, not an object of charity-he does not wish to be that-but he does think, and I think with him, that the people of Canada might well, through their Government, place an amount in the Estimates which would in a measure assist him in bearing the affliction that has come upon him on account of his work for the benefit of Canada during the Northwest rebellion. I know that this case has been brought before the Militia Department under the late Government as well as this Government, and the ground has been taken that there is no legal claim, as he was

not really an employee of the Militia Department, though in substance he contends he was. I admit that at once. If anything is to be given, it must come under the heading of what we call a compassionate allowance, and not through any Tight. I know that last year the minister took the ground that it might establish a precedent. I do not think it would establish any precedent, but I would go so far as to say that if any other case arose that was on all fours with this case, I would grant gladly and support a compassionate allowance. He did this work, he became subject to this life-long affliction, the terrible one of blindness, at a time when men in employment such as , hits had no opportunity of being surrounded with such safeguards as they have now; there were no Workmen's Compensation Acts of which a man could take advantage in order that he might be protected if injured. He did his duty, and, taking the hours he worked day and night, he did not receive as much pay as an ordinary soldier does at the present time. I am pleading his case not on any legal ground, I am not suggesting that he has a legal claim, but as one which might be properly expressed in the words compassionate allowance. I believe that no precedent would be established by giving him a small amount, and I plead with the Government to place in the Supplementary Estimates for next year an amount which they think fair and proper in order that this man may be helped through the balance of his life to enjoy himself as much as possible with this great affliction. I asked him to put a statement fairly from his own standpoint, and this is what he has given me:
I was turned over to the Militia Department at Ottawa with instructions to report to Colonel Jackson. My wages, transportation, and expenses were paid by the Militia Department until I returned to Ottawa. I received orders from Colonel Jackson to report to Colonel Forrest at Qu'Appelle. I was under that gentleman's orders until the rebellion was suppressed. If it will he necessary to take it up in the House, the thing should he considered.
First, I worked day and night to assist the expedition, and when you consider overtime I did not receive as much as a private soldier to-day.
Second, I lost my eyesight through exposure in connection with the Northwest rebellion. That has been proven by certificates furnished by Dr. Edwards, Government [DOT] officer, Qu'Appelle, and Dr. Horsey, Ottawa.
How old is he?

I do not know, but I
should think that he is forty-five or fifty
years o-ld.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
This case has
been before me for consideration. I understand that it was brought 'before the Militia Department during the period of the late Government, and also since the present Government assumed office. There -seems no doubt that under the regulations of the Militia Department this unfortunate man would not be entitled to a pension. As my hon. friend has- said, there is no legal claim. He was not a member of the militia force; he was not, so far as the facts are in my information paid by .the Government; he was in private employ. He was a telegrapher in the employ of the Canadian -Pacific Railway at the time of the Northwest rebellion. I believe that even if he had been a member of the militia he would not be legally entitled to a pension because of -the period which has elapsed.
That is not his fault.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There is, of
course, good reason for the rule which debars a man after a certain time because there is uncertainty in relating his affliction to his service -at so remote a date; there is always an element of uncertainty in those cases which are brought forward after a lapse of years. So that on legal grounds or under the regulations of the Militia Department he clearly would not be entitled to consideration for pension. My hon. friend recognizes that, and puts -forward the case as one for compassionate allowance on the part of the Government. In admitting a case of that kind we must have regard to principle and to precedent, which -must necessarily be established. My difficulty in regard to this case has not been one of lack of sympathy fpr him, because I think it is a hard case. This man is heavily afflicted, being blind, and our sympathies naturally go out to him. But when we consider putting him upon the pension -list of the Dominion, we have to proceed in accordance with some principle, otherwise -we should establish a precedent which would be embarrassing to ourselves and to succeeding Governments in matters of this kind. If the man was in private employ, I cannot see on what principle we can place him upon the list of those to whom the Government has granted pensions on the ground of compassionate allowance. One naturally considers just what the adoption of that principle would lead to. We take -the case of a man who is engaged by a railway company as an engineer or brake-man or other employee in connection with the
*bringing up of supplies for am -army in time of war. Supposing that he was injured; could you rightly differentiate his case from the case of -this unfortunate man? Take the case even of an operative who is injured to-day in a munitions factory. He is in private employ, but nevertheless he is doing work indirectly or even directly connected with the carrying on of . the war. My 'hon. friend will realize the questions that might arise -from the establishment of a precedent of this character. My hon, friend has stated that he has been informed that this man was sent out to the Northwest by the Mil-itia Department and paid by the Militia Department. If that is so, -that has not been brought to my attention. If my hon. friend can establish that I will be glad to look into the ease again, although I shall not commit myself and cannot, of course, -commit the Government to any course of action.
That is a new statement, so far as I am concerned. My hon. friend from South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) and Dr. Maloney have brought this case to my attention, and so far I have been unable to see on what principle I could admit this man, although, so far as my own sympathies are concerned, I would like to do so. I am afraid, however, that a precedent might be established that would be quite unsound, and that would commit this and succeeding Governments to similar action on what might possibly be a large scale.

I will try to get the information.

Ross, who was a very valuable member of the staff of the Finance Department, and who acted most acceptably as deputy minister for many years, resigned in order to take a much more lucrative position with the Canadian Bankers' Association. I filled the vacancy by promoting Mr. Saunders, who has been the Dominion bookkeeper for many years, a very capable official.
And deserving of promotion.

speechtext: I adopted the principle of promotion, and Mr. Saunders occupies the position which a couple of months ago was occupied by a Mr. Ross.
What is the salary of the secretary?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My private secretary, Mr. Veitz, has gone to the front. He left the service of the department last spring. I took a young man on in his place, and he is now acting as my secretary. For some months he acted as assistant secretary, and the salary which he was getting was, I think, something like $1,300. I took him on as my secretary, and he becomes entitled to the secretarial allowance of $600, that is $300 for the period of six months ending 31st March of this year.

I am not against the increase of salaries, hut if the minister finds it necessary to make an increase of $500 in the case of his deputy minister, and increases the salary of his secretary from $1,300 to $1,600, I would ask if it would not be possible for him to put an item in the estimates increasing the salaries of the letter carriers, not only in Montreal, but all over Canada. He knows very well that the cost of living has 'increased, and that those letter carriers get a salary of $900 a year. There is no better class of employees in the Government service. They work 365 days in the year, working on New Year's Day and on Christmas Day. I think that these * men are deserving of an increase because the cost of living to-day is so high, being more than 100 per cent in different articles than it was before. The man who is getting $900 a year to-day is really not getting more than $450. If the big salaries have to be increased the small ones ought to he increased also, and those who are getting $750, $800 and $900 should receive the consideration of the Minister of Finance. I am not speaking only for the letter carriers of Montreal, but for all the letter carriers in Canada. Their wage is a email one, and it should be increased .at this time. They have asked the Government to do so, but have received no answer yet.

Minister of Customs
speechtext: The hon. member knows that Mr. Verret is at the front, and while he is away there has to be an Assistant Deputy Postmaster General.

speechtext: I think it is all right.

speechtext:
The item as it
appears in the Estimates is precisely as it came from the department. I do not think for one moment that any change has been made in the status of Major Verret. Whether Mr. Fowler is Assistant Deputy Postmaster

General or not, I am not prepared to say, but I shall draw the attention of the Postmaster General to the matter. I do not believe that this item would make him Assistant Deputy Postmaster General-'if he was not. I am sorry that the Postmaster General is not here, .as I am not in a position to give my hon. friend any information.

I should like to support the remarks of the hon. member for St. MaTy's (Mr. Martin) in respect to some extra allowance being given to postal carriers in some of the cities at least, if not in all I think it is a case deserving the consideration of the Government. I understand that the matter has been placed before them by the Postal Carriers' Association and that possibly it will receive the favourable consideration of the Government. Therefore, I merely wish to concur in the suggestion of the hon, member for Montreal, St. Mary's (Mr. Martin) that something ought to be done for them either in the way of an increase in. salary or a bonus or something of that nature. The Minister of Finance made a remark in answer to the statement made by my hon. friend from South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) in which he asked for a compassionate allowance for a certain person in the province of Ontario. On page 5 of the Estimates I find:
Allowance to Emile Carrier for injuries which resulted in the loss of an eye. . . $600.
This in the nature of a compassionate allowance. The Minister of Finance suggested a moment'ago that these votes should be based upon some principle. I brought to the attention of the Department of Railways and Canals the case of a young man in Halifax who was in the employ of that department. About a year agO' a fire occurred in a shed upon one of the piers of the Intercolonial railway. This employee was at his home and had retired for the night when he was called out by his chief at the freight shed to fight the fire. Whi'a so engaged he lost his life. The matter has been brought to the attention of the Prime Minister, and the Minister of Railways and Canals and the Department of Railways and Canals was kind enough to advise me the other day that this young man was being allowed $500. Here is the case where a young man is taken from his home after his working hours, is engaged in protecting
the property of the Government, and loses his life and it is proposed to vote a compassionate allowance of $500. On the other hand, here is a case where $600 is proposed to be voted to a man for the loss of an eye. I am not objecting to it, but it does seem to me there is a variance in the application of the principle as between these two cases. I hope the day will soon come when we can take care of the employees of governments in a more scientific fashion than we are doing to-day. In almost all of the provinces we have the Workmen's Compensation Act but, it cannot provide for the employees of the Government and I hope we may establish some protection in the nature of the Workmen's Compensation Act for the employees of the Government who may meet with accidents. I refer to the matter to show that there is a very material distinction made between these two cases and I trust that the Minister of Railways and Canals will remember my observations to-night and look into the case further.
Did the young man leave any dependents?
He did not leave any dependents except that he was a substantial contributor to the upkeep of his home and parents.

This afternoon I made an inquiry of the right hon. the Prime Minister to know whether a postmaster at Montreal has been appointed. I see there are three vacancies in the higher outside Civil Service at Montreal-the collector of the port of Montreal and the postmaster of Montreal and the inspector of weights and measures. The three most important offices in the outside Civil Service are now vacant in Montreal. Whilst it is none of my business to recommend to the Government who ought to be appointed, I may be allowed to say a word or two about what public opinion considers to be the proper disposition of these offices. First of all, I wish tc ^ay that the post office lost an excellent official in the death of the late Mr. Bergeron. He was a kindly and courteous gentleman, he was in his office every day, the public had access to him, and really, he is lamented by the whole population of Montreal. We all know his geniality and his great courtesy towards the public and he will be hard to replace. Yet, if the Government would accept my recommendation, I would say first of all proceed by way of promotion. There are excellent officers in the office in Montreal. For instance, there

is Mr. Gaboury, who started at almost the lowest rung of the ladder and who now holds the office of post office inspector for the eastern section of Canada, a district extending from Montreal to Halifax. I am quite sure that his appointment would be very popular with the business men of Montreal. There is also in the post office Mr. Barcelo, who is very active, land who has taken a great interest in his work since he has been appointed. Of course, if the Government will go outside, there are some very excellent names. There is my friend Mr. Robillard, editor of La Patrie, who is a good fellow, who served his country in the Northwest rebellion, who has been in journalism for thirty years, who is, in fact, one of the deans of the press in Montreal and who is certainly entitled to some recognition at the hands of his political friends. Then, there is Mr. H. A. Cholette, K.C., a fighter of the old days who would, I am sure, be an excellent postmaster of Montreal. I have a certain sympathy with him because he belongs to the same profession as I do and if the Government appoint him I think it will be a very popular appointment.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: Appoint them all.
There are many more. I understand that my hon. friend for Montcalm (Mr. Lafortune) has some recommendations to make also.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: Have you a preference for any of these that you have named?

No, any of them would satisfy me; any one of them would make an excellent postmaster and would be an ornament to the office. As regards the Customs, I think the Government 12 and the country have sus-
Midnight. tained a real loss in the resignation of Mr. White who was for many years the member for Cardwell in the House of Commons. For twenty-one years he has been collector of the largest port in Canada and everybody agrees that he has fulfilled his duties to the satisfaction of the minister, of the Government, and of the public in general. There again the Government can proceed by way of promotion. The name of Mr. McLaughlin, one of the chief officials at the port of Montreal, has been mentioned and I think the name will be well received by the business com-' munity. As regards the inspector of weights and measures, as some names have been mentioned from among members of the

House of Commons, I shall make no comment here. But if one hon. member whose name has been mentioned gets the appointment, I will give him my blessing and say to the Government that they have made a good appointment.
This money has all been expended; it is not for expenditure in the future?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Or that will be expended before the 31st of March.
It is for this year; it is not for next year?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: For this year.
I find that nearly all of it is for the operation of the Government railways.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: That is right.

That means, it is money that will he returned to the Treasury, but that has to be voted.
Reverting again to my suggestion to the Minister of Finance, I take it for granted that he has net shut the. door more tightly in regard to the McNab case and that he is going to give if some consideration during recess, and that I am going to receive some information from him on this subject.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I shall he only too glad to take into consideration anything that my hon. friend may submit.

I have no letter carriers in my constituency, but I am pleased to support the suggestion made by the hon. member of St. Mary's, Montreal (Mr. Martin) in that connection. There was a petition circulated on behalf of the letter carriers and they sent their representatives around in various counties. One of them was sent to me from a branch of the association in the city of Sydney, and I replied saying that if the matter came up in the House of Commons I would give it my sympathetic support. As has already been pointed out, the pay of these men was fixed some years ago when the cost of living was about half what it is to-day. These men have been in the business for quite a while, and as it is not so easy for a man to get away from a position in which he has established himself, I think that, having regard to the fact that the cost of living for these' men and their families has more than doubled, they deserve the consideration of the Government as to whether or not some further remuneration should he given to them.

May I ask my hon. friend the Minister of Finance if any decision has been reached in regard to the increase, more or less promised, but hinted some years ago, to the Civil Service? I understand that lately the Government received a delegation from the Civil Service Association, which laid a request before the Government. I know that we are passing through hard times an'cHtbat the expenditures of the country are high, but the man who suffers most in these days from the high cost of living is really the man who has nothing to depend upon but his fixed salary.
Has my hon. friend'considered the position in which the Civil Service is to-day? And does he intend to do something about it? Three years ago, just before the war, he

had a tender spot in his heart for the Civil Service. Perhaps, in Bis anxiety about the war, he may have overlooked the poor civil servant. I cannot forget that I am the son of a civil servant myself, and I know what the anxieties of the poor civil servants are. We all expect a word of hope from the Minister of Finance on behalf of this class of employees.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
In the midst of a war such as this, and with the burdens that are thrust upon the public, the time is not very opportune for considering a revision of the Civil Service salary list. But we are all aware that the cost of living has gone up during the past few years, especially since the outbreak of the war. It is altogether probable that when the House resumes after the recess we shall deal with the questions of the salaries at least of the lower grades of the Service. The matter has been under consideration.

speechtext: On the motion of Sir Thomas White for the adjournment of the House:

Before the House
adjourns,. I wish to say a word about the coal situation.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: With the leave of the House.

With the leave of the House, of course, because I consider this a very important question. I reported to the Minister of Railways this evening that several consignees were complaining that coal consigned to private firms was being confiscated by certain railway companies-and I named one of the companies-much to the detriment of private industry in Canada.
* My hon. friend has been good enough to notify the company named to respect the rights of private firms, and I thank him for what he did. Had it not been for the happy intervention of the hon. minister, a very important pulp establishment would have been obliged to close its doors, and leave about 800 hands inactive, incurring thereby a loss of about $10,000 daily. As the complaint seems to be general, I would like my hon. friend to give the House and the country a pronouncement on the subject. Can any railway company, by this high-handed action

I shall not say abuse its privileges, because such a privilege does not belong to it-deprive its customers of property of which they stand greatly in need?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
I think the railways vhave the right to do this, because trains must be kept moving. The stopping of the trains would more seriously discommode the public than the action to which my hon. friend refers.	There is, no doubt,
great	scarcity of coal all over
Canada; the Intercolonial railway itself has had to take coal belonging to other people. The coal companies have not been able to get the necessary number of men to enable them to fill their contracts. We ourselves have had to bring in some
500,000	tons of coal. I am sure that the company that took this coal is in a very bad way; in fact, all the Canadian railways are in a bad way in different localities. As I told the hon. gentleman, I wired the president of the company to which he referred and asked him to try and let up so that the different industries could be

kept going. I shall be very glad to do anything that I can in the matter.
